answer: A classic external script without async or defer can block HTML parsing while the browser downloads and executes the script. This can delay page rendering and DOM construction, which is why script placement and loading strategy are important for performance.

title: What is the difference between async, defer, and module scripts?
answer: Classic scripts without special attributes can block parsing. defer downloads scripts while parsing and executes them after parsing in document order. async executes as soon as the script is available. Scripts with type="module" are deferred by default, support JavaScript modules, and have module-specific loading and execution behavior.

title: What is the purpose of the meta viewport tag?
answer: The viewport meta tag controls how a page's viewport is interpreted on mobile devices. A common configuration is <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">. It allows responsive layouts to use the device's actual viewport width rather than a wider virtual layout viewport.

title: What is the difference between absolute, relative, and canonical URLs in HTML?
answer: An absolute URL contains the complete scheme and host, such as https://example.com/products. A relative URL is resolved relative to the current document or base URL, such as products/item.html. A canonical URL identifies the preferred URL for a resource and is commonly specified using a <link rel="canonical"> element.

title: What is the purpose of the base element in HTML?
answer: The <base> element specifies the base URL and optionally the default browsing context for relative URLs in a document. Because it affects how relative URLs are resolved throughout the document, it should be used carefully.

title: What is the difference between iframe and object elements?
answer: <iframe> embeds another browsing context, commonly used for documents or external web content. <object> is a more general embedding element that can represent external resources such as documents or other media. For embedding another webpage, <iframe> is generally the more appropriate element.

title: What is the purpose of the lang attribute in HTML?
answer: The lang attribute specifies the language of the document or an element's content. For example, <html lang="en"> indicates English. It helps screen readers, search engines, translation tools, and browsers correctly interpret the content.

title: What is the dir attribute in HTML?
answer: The dir attribute specifies the direction of text. Common values are ltr for left-to-right and rtl for right-to-left. It is particularly useful when supporting languages such as Arabic and Hebrew.

title: What is the difference between hidden and display:none?
answer: The hidden HTML attribute semantically indicates that an element is not currently relevant or should not be presented to the user. display: none is a CSS presentation rule that removes the element from the rendered layout. The two mechanisms can produce similar visual results but serve different purposes.

title: What is the purpose of the tabindex attribute?
answer: The tabindex attribute controls whether an element can receive keyboard focus and its position in sequential keyboard navigation. A value of 0 generally includes an element in the natural tab order, while a negative value allows programmatic focus without adding it to the normal tab sequence.

title: What is the difference between tabindex="0" and tabindex="-1"?
answer: tabindex="0" allows an element to participate in the natural keyboard tab order. tabindex="-1" removes the element from sequential keyboard navigation but still allows it to receive programmatic focus using JavaScript.

title: What is the purpose of the aria-label attribute?
answer: aria-label provides an accessible name for an element when a suitable visible text label is not available. It should be used carefully because visible labels are generally preferable when they can provide the accessible name naturally.

title: What is the difference between aria-label and aria-labelledby?
answer: aria-label directly provides an accessible name as a string. aria-labelledby references one or more existing elements whose text provides the accessible name. When visible text already exists, aria-labelledby can often provide a better semantic relationship.

title: What is the purpose of the role attribute in HTML?
answer: The role attribute communicates an element's semantic role to accessibility technologies. Native HTML elements should generally be preferred because they already provide appropriate semantics. ARIA roles are most useful when native HTML cannot express the required behavior or semantics.

title: Why should semantic HTML be preferred over excessive ARIA?
answer: Native semantic HTML provides built-in accessibility semantics and browser behavior. Excessive or incorrect ARIA can introduce accessibility problems rather than solving them. A good principle is to use the appropriate native HTML element first and add ARIA only when necessary.

title: What is the purpose of the dialog element in HTML5?
answer: The <dialog> element represents a dialog or interactive modal-like component. JavaScript can use methods such as show() and showModal() to display it and close() to close it. It provides native semantics for dialog interfaces.

title: What is the difference between dialog.show() and dialog.showModal()?
answer: show() displays a dialog as a non-modal dialog, allowing interaction with the rest of the document. showModal() displays it as a modal dialog, creating a modal interaction state where the rest of the document is not normally interactive until the dialog is closed.

title: What is the purpose of the details and summary elements?
answer: The <details> element represents a disclosure widget, while <summary> provides its visible heading or control. Users can expand or collapse the content without requiring custom JavaScript for the basic interaction.

title: What is the purpose of the output element in HTML5?
answer: The <output> element represents the result of a calculation or user action. It is useful for displaying dynamically calculated values, such as the result of multiplying quantity and price in a form.

title: What is the purpose of the datalist element?
answer: The <datalist> element provides a set of suggested options for an input. An input can reference the datalist through its list attribute. Unlike a select element, the user can generally enter a value that is not included in the suggestions.

title: What is the difference between select and datalist?
answer: A <select> element restricts the user to choosing from its available options unless additional behavior is implemented. A <datalist> provides suggestions for an associated input but normally allows the user to enter a value that is not included in the suggestions.

title: What is the purpose of the meter element in HTML5?
answer: The <meter> element represents a scalar measurement within a known range, such as disk usage, a score, or a confidence value. It is different from <progress>, which represents the completion progress of a task.

title: What is the difference between progress and meter elements?
answer: <progress> represents the completion progress of a task, such as a file upload. <meter> represents a measurement within a known range, such as a score, rating, or resource usage level.

title: What is the purpose of the time element in HTML5?
answer: The <time> element represents a specific period, date, time, or duration in a machine-readable way. The optional datetime attribute can provide a machine-readable representation while the element's text provides the human-readable form.

title: What is the purpose of the mark element in HTML5?
answer: The <mark> element represents text that is highlighted or marked because it is relevant in the current context. For example, search results can use <mark> to highlight the portion of text matching a user's search query.

title: What is the difference between ol, ul, and dl elements?
answer: <ol> represents an ordered list where sequence matters. <ul> represents an unordered list where sequence is not inherently important. <dl> represents a description list consisting of terms and their corresponding descriptions, typically using <dt> and <dd>.

title: What is the purpose of the main element in HTML5?
answer: The <main> element represents the primary content of a document. A page should generally have one main content area, excluding repeated content such as navigation, headers, and footers. It also provides useful semantic information for accessibility technologies.

title: What is the difference between nav and menu elements?
answer: The <nav> element represents a section containing navigation links. The <menu> element represents a list of commands or menu items and has a different semantic purpose. For typical website navigation, <nav> is the appropriate element.

title: What is the purpose of the aside element?
answer: The <aside> element represents content that is tangentially related to the surrounding content. Examples include sidebars, related articles, advertisements, or supplementary information.

title: What is the difference between figure and img elements?
answer: <img> embeds an image resource, while <figure> represents self-contained content such as an image, diagram, chart, or code example. A <figcaption> can provide a caption for the content inside a figure.

title: What is the purpose of the figcaption element?
answer: The <figcaption> element provides a caption or description for content contained within a <figure>. It can be used with images, diagrams, charts, code examples, or other self-contained content.

title: What is the difference between article and section in HTML5?
answer: An <article> represents a self-contained piece of content that could potentially be distributed independently, such as a blog post or news item. A <section> represents a thematic grouping of related content. An article can contain multiple sections.

title: Can a section contain an article and can an article contain a section?
answer: Yes. HTML's semantic elements can be nested based on the meaning of the content. An article can contain multiple sections, and a section can contain articles when those articles form part of the section's thematic content.

title: What is the purpose of the address element?
answer: The <address> element represents contact information for the nearest article or the entire document. It can contain information such as an email address, author contact details, or other relevant contact information.

title: What is the difference between blockquote and q elements?
answer: <blockquote> represents an extended quotation, typically displayed as a separate block of content. <q> represents a short inline quotation. The cite attribute can optionally provide the URL of the source.

title: What is the purpose of the cite element?
answer: The <cite> element represents the title of a referenced creative work, such as a book, movie, article, or research paper. It provides semantic meaning rather than simply applying a visual style.

title: What is the purpose of the abbr element?
answer: The <abbr> element represents an abbreviation or acronym. The title attribute can provide the expanded form. For example, <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> identifies the abbreviation and its full meaning.

title: What is the difference between br and hr elements?
answer: <br> represents a line break within text, while <hr> represents a thematic break between sections of content. Neither should be used simply for visual spacing; CSS should be used for layout spacing.

title: Why should HTML entities be used in HTML?
answer: HTML character references allow reserved characters and special characters to be represented safely in markup. For example, < represents the less-than character and & represents an ampersand. They are especially useful when characters could otherwise be interpreted as HTML markup.

title: What is the difference between absolute and relative paths for images and links?
answer: An absolute URL specifies the complete resource location, such as https://example.com/images/logo.png. A relative URL is resolved relative to the current document or base URL, such as images/logo.png. Relative paths are commonly used for resources within the same website.

title: What is the purpose of rel="noopener" on external links?
answer: rel="noopener" prevents a newly opened browsing context from accessing the opener through window.opener. It is useful when opening links in a new browsing context and helps protect against certain reverse-tabnabbing scenarios.

title: What is the purpose of the target="_blank" attribute?
answer: target="_blank" requests that the linked resource be opened in a new browsing context, such as a new tab or window. When using it for external links, appropriate rel values such as noopener should be considered for security.

title: What is the difference between noreferrer and noopener?
answer: noopener prevents the opened page from accessing the opener through window.opener. noreferrer additionally prevents the browser from sending the referring page's URL in the HTTP Referer header and generally implies the opener protection associated with noopener.

title: What is the purpose of the crossorigin attribute?
answer: The crossorigin attribute controls how certain resources, such as images, scripts, and media, participate in cross-origin requests. Depending on the element and value, it can cause the browser to perform a CORS-enabled request and determine whether the resource can be used in contexts such as Canvas.

title: What is Subresource Integrity in HTML?
answer: Subresource Integrity, or SRI, allows a page to specify a cryptographic hash for an external resource such as a JavaScript or CSS file. The browser can verify that the downloaded resource matches the expected hash before using it. It is commonly used when loading third-party assets from CDNs.

title: How do you improve HTML page performance without changing the application logic?
answer: Use semantic and efficient markup, optimize images, use responsive image techniques, lazy-load suitable resources, minimize unnecessary DOM nodes, defer non-critical scripts, preload critical resources when justified, use appropriate caching and CDN strategies, and avoid render-blocking resources where possible. Performance should be measured using browser developer tools and real-user metrics rather than relying only on assumptions.

title: What is the difference between semantic and non-semantic HTML elements?
answer: Semantic elements describe the meaning and purpose of their content, such as <article>, <nav>, and <main>. Non-semantic elements such as <div> and <span> do not describe the meaning of their content. Semantic HTML improves accessibility, maintainability, and document structure.

title: What is the difference between HTML validation and accessibility validation?
answer: HTML validation checks whether markup follows the applicable HTML syntax and specification requirements. Accessibility validation checks whether the page can be effectively used by people with disabilities, including keyboard users and screen-reader users. Valid HTML is important, but valid markup alone does not guarantee accessibility.

title: What are ARIA attributes and when should they be used?
answer: ARIA attributes provide additional accessibility semantics for dynamic or custom user-interface components. They should be used when native HTML semantics cannot adequately describe the component. Developers should prefer native HTML elements whenever possible and avoid adding ARIA roles or states that conflict with native semantics.

title: What is the difference between aria-hidden="true" and the hidden attribute?
answer: aria-hidden="true" removes an element from the accessibility tree while it can potentially remain visually visible. The hidden attribute indicates that the element is not currently relevant and is normally not rendered. Therefore, they should not be treated as interchangeable.

title: Why should you avoid putting interactive elements inside other interactive elements?
answer: Nesting interactive elements such as placing a button inside a link can create ambiguous keyboard behavior, confusing accessibility semantics, and invalid or problematic interaction patterns. Each interactive control should generally have a clear and independent purpose.

title: What is the difference between button and anchor elements?
answer: A <button> represents an action, such as submitting a form, opening a dialog, or triggering application behavior. An <a> element represents navigation to another resource or location. Using the correct element provides appropriate keyboard behavior and accessibility semantics.

title: Why should you use a button instead of a div for clickable actions?
answer: A native <button> provides built-in keyboard interaction, focus behavior, semantics, and form integration. A clickable <div> requires additional keyboard handling, focus management, and accessibility semantics. Therefore, a button is usually the correct choice for an interactive action.

title: What is the purpose of the autocomplete attribute on input elements?
answer: The autocomplete attribute gives browsers and password managers hints about the expected type of information. Values such as username, current-password, new-password, email, and tel can improve autofill behavior and user experience.

title: What is the purpose of inputmode in HTML5?
answer: The inputmode attribute provides a hint about the virtual keyboard that should be displayed on devices with on-screen keyboards. For example, inputmode="numeric" can request a numeric keyboard. It does not itself enforce validation or change the input's underlying type.

title: What is the difference between input type="number" and inputmode="numeric"?
answer: type="number" defines the semantic type of the form control and provides number-oriented browser behavior and validation. inputmode="numeric" is primarily a hint about the virtual keyboard to display. If the value is not semantically a number, such as a postal code, a text input with an appropriate input mode may be more suitable.

title: What is the purpose of the autocomplete="off" attribute?
answer: autocomplete="off" indicates that the page does not want the browser to automatically fill or suggest previously entered values. However, browsers and password managers may make their own decisions in certain security-sensitive contexts, so developers should not assume that the attribute universally disables all autofill behavior.

title: What is the difference between minlength and maxlength?
answer: minlength specifies the minimum number of characters allowed in applicable text controls, while maxlength specifies the maximum number of characters. These attributes participate in the browser's constraint validation system.

title: What is the difference between min and minlength in HTML forms?
answer: min specifies a minimum numeric, date, or time value for applicable input types. minlength specifies the minimum number of characters for applicable text controls. They validate different characteristics of the input.

title: What is the purpose of the pattern attribute?
answer: The pattern attribute specifies a regular expression that the value of an applicable input must satisfy for constraint validation to succeed. It is useful for formats such as identifiers or custom text patterns, but server-side validation is still required because client-side validation can be bypassed.

title: What is the Constraint Validation API?
answer: The Constraint Validation API provides JavaScript interfaces for interacting with built-in HTML form validation. Methods and properties such as checkValidity(), reportValidity(), setCustomValidity(), and validity allow developers to inspect and control validation behavior.

title: What is the difference between checkValidity() and reportValidity()?
answer: checkValidity() checks whether a form or control satisfies its validation constraints and returns a boolean. reportValidity() performs the validation check and, when invalid, allows the browser to report the validation problem to the user through its native validation UI.

title: What is setCustomValidity() used for?
answer: setCustomValidity() allows JavaScript to define a custom validation message for a form control. Passing a non-empty string makes the control invalid, while passing an empty string clears the custom error and allows the normal validation rules to determine validity.

title: What is the purpose of the formnovalidate attribute?
answer: The formnovalidate attribute on a submit button tells the browser not to perform constraint validation when that particular button submits the form. It is useful when a form provides an alternate action, such as saving a draft, that should bypass normal validation.

title: What is the purpose of the novalidate attribute on a form?
answer: The novalidate attribute disables the browser's built-in constraint validation when the form is submitted. It can be useful when an application implements its own validation system, although developers should ensure that the custom validation provides an accessible and robust user experience.

title: How would you build an accessible and performant HTML5 form?
answer: I would use semantic form elements, associate every control with an appropriate label, provide clear validation messages, use native input types and constraints where suitable, support keyboard navigation, maintain visible focus indicators, use appropriate autocomplete and inputmode values, optimize resource loading, and avoid unnecessary DOM complexity. I would also test the form with keyboard navigation, screen readers, different viewport sizes, and automated accessibility tools.

title: What is the purpose of the iframe sandbox attribute?
answer: The sandbox attribute applies additional restrictions to content loaded inside an <iframe>. Restrictions can include preventing scripts, form submission, navigation, or origin privileges. Specific capabilities can be selectively enabled using sandbox tokens such as allow-scripts and allow-forms.

title: What is the difference between sandbox and allow attributes on an iframe?
answer: sandbox applies a set of restrictions to the embedded browsing context, while the allow attribute controls permissions for specific browser features through Permissions Policy. They solve different security and capability-control problems.

title: What is the purpose of the referrerpolicy attribute?
answer: The referrerpolicy attribute controls how much referrer information the browser sends when navigating to or fetching a resource. Policies such as no-referrer, origin, and strict-origin-when-cross-origin allow developers to control referrer information for privacy and security.

title: What is the purpose of the download attribute on an anchor element?
answer: The download attribute indicates that the linked resource is intended to be downloaded rather than navigated to. An optional value can suggest a filename. Browser behavior can vary depending on the resource, origin, and response headers.

title: What is the purpose of the hreflang attribute?
answer: The hreflang attribute identifies the language and, optionally, regional targeting of an alternate version of a page. It is commonly used with <link> elements to help search engines understand localized versions of content.

title: What is the difference between rel="canonical" and hreflang?
answer: rel="canonical" identifies the preferred URL among duplicate or substantially similar pages. hreflang identifies alternate localized or language-specific versions of a page. Canonicalization and internationalization solve different SEO problems.

title: What is the purpose of meta description in HTML?
answer: The meta name="description" element provides a concise description of the page. Search engines may use it as a snippet in search results, although they can choose different text depending on the query and page content.

title: What is the difference between meta charset and Content-Type charset?
answer: The <meta charset="UTF-8"> element declares the character encoding from within the HTML document. An HTTP Content-Type response header can also specify the encoding. The HTTP response header is authoritative when present, while the HTML declaration provides an important early declaration for document parsing.

title: Why is UTF-8 commonly used in HTML5 documents?
answer: UTF-8 can represent characters from a very large range of writing systems and symbols and is widely supported across browsers, servers, and development tools. Using UTF-8 consistently helps prevent character-encoding problems when displaying multilingual content.

title: What is the purpose of the meta robots tag?
answer: The meta robots tag provides search-engine crawling and indexing instructions for a page. Common directives include noindex, nofollow, and noarchive. These directives should be used carefully because they affect how search engines handle the page.

title: What is the purpose of the link rel="preload" attribute?
answer: rel="preload" tells the browser that a resource is important and should be fetched early because it is expected to be needed soon. It can be useful for critical fonts, scripts, styles, or images, but excessive preloading can waste bandwidth and hurt performance.

title: What is the difference between preload and prefetch?
answer: preload is intended for resources that the current page is expected to need soon and gives them higher loading priority. prefetch is generally a lower-priority hint for resources that may be needed by a future navigation or later interaction.

title: What is the purpose of rel="preconnect"?
answer: rel="preconnect" allows the browser to establish an early connection to an origin that is expected to provide critical resources. This can reduce connection setup latency for resources loaded from third-party origins, such as fonts or CDN assets.

title: What is the purpose of the srcset attribute on script elements?
answer: The standard srcset attribute is primarily associated with responsive images rather than general script loading. For scripts, responsive resource selection is generally handled through other mechanisms such as module loading, conditional logic, or build-system output. Therefore, srcset should not be treated as a general-purpose script-loading feature.

title: What is the difference between script type="module" and a classic script?
answer: A module script supports ES module syntax such as import and export, is deferred by default, and has module-specific scoping and loading behavior. A classic script does not provide module semantics and normally executes according to its placement and async or defer attributes.

title: What is the purpose of the nomodule attribute?
answer: The nomodule attribute allows a classic script to be provided as a fallback for browsers that do not support JavaScript modules. Module-supporting browsers generally skip the nomodule script.

title: What is the purpose of the type="module" attribute when using React or modern JavaScript?
answer: type="module" enables the browser's native JavaScript module system, allowing the script to use import and export. Modern build tools such as Vite or other bundlers commonly generate module-based scripts as part of the production application.

title: What is the purpose of the template element in HTML5?
answer: The <template> element contains HTML that is not rendered immediately. Its contents can be cloned and inserted into the document using JavaScript. It is useful for defining reusable markup structures and is also an important building block for Web Components.

title: What is the difference between template content and normal DOM content?
answer: Content inside a <template> element is stored in a separate document fragment and is not rendered as part of the document until it is explicitly cloned or inserted. Normal DOM content participates directly in rendering and layout.

title: What are Web Components and how do they relate to HTML5?
answer: Web Components are a set of browser standards for building reusable custom elements. They commonly use Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, HTML templates, and related platform APIs. They allow developers to create reusable UI components without requiring a specific JavaScript framework.

title: What is CSS and what was introduced with CSS3?
answer: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets and is used to control the presentation and layout of HTML documents. CSS3 introduced many modern capabilities through modules, including transitions, animations, transforms, gradients, flexible layouts, grid layouts, media queries, and advanced selectors.

title: What is the CSS box model?
answer: The CSS box model describes how an element's dimensions are calculated using four areas: content, padding, border, and margin. By default, width and height apply to the content box. The box-sizing property can change this behavior.

title: What is the difference between content-box and border-box?
answer: With box-sizing: content-box, the declared width and height apply only to the content area, so padding and borders increase the final rendered size. With box-sizing: border-box, the declared width and height include the content, padding, and border.

title: What is CSS specificity?
answer: Specificity determines which CSS declaration wins when multiple rules target the same element. In general, inline styles have higher specificity than IDs, IDs have higher specificity than classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes, and those have higher specificity than element and pseudo-element selectors. When specificity is equal, the later applicable declaration wins.

title: What is the CSS cascade?
answer: The CSS cascade is the process browsers use to determine which declarations apply when multiple rules match an element. It considers factors such as origin and importance, cascade layers, specificity, and source order. The cascade allows styles from different sources and components to work together predictably.

title: What is the difference between inline, internal, and external CSS?
answer: Inline CSS is written directly in an element's style attribute. Internal CSS is placed inside a <style> element within the document. External CSS is stored in a separate stylesheet and referenced using a <link> element. External stylesheets are generally preferred for maintainability and reuse.

title: What is the difference between relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky positioning?
answer: relative keeps the element in normal flow while allowing it to be offset. absolute removes the element from normal flow and positions it relative to an appropriate containing block. fixed positions the element relative to the viewport in typical cases. sticky behaves like a relatively positioned element until a specified scroll threshold is reached, after which it behaves like a stuck element within its containing context.

title: What is the difference between display:none, visibility:hidden, and opacity:0?
answer: display: none removes the element from the layout. visibility: hidden keeps the element's layout space but hides it. opacity: 0 makes the element fully transparent while it generally remains in layout and can still participate in interaction unless additional properties prevent that behavior.

title: What is Flexbox and when would you use it?
answer: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system designed to arrange items along a row or column. It is useful for navigation bars, toolbars, alignment, spacing, responsive components, and layouts where content needs to distribute dynamically along one primary axis.

title: What is CSS Grid and when would you use it?
answer: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system that works with rows and columns. It is useful for complex page layouts, dashboards, card grids, and interfaces where both horizontal and vertical relationships need explicit control.

title: What is the difference between Flexbox and CSS Grid?
answer: Flexbox is primarily designed for one-dimensional layouts, where items are arranged along a single main axis. Grid is designed for two-dimensional layouts involving both rows and columns. In real applications they are often used together, with Grid handling larger page structures and Flexbox handling component-level alignment.

title: What is the difference between justify-content and align-items in Flexbox?
answer: justify-content controls how flex items are distributed along the main axis. align-items controls their alignment along the cross axis. The actual physical direction depends on the flex container's flex-direction.

title: What is the difference between align-items and align-content?
answer: align-items aligns individual flex or grid items within the cross axis. align-content controls the distribution of multiple flex lines or grid tracks within the container when there is extra space. align-content has an effect only when there is extra cross-axis space and multiple lines or tracks are involved.

title: What are CSS pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements?
answer: Pseudo-classes represent a state or condition of an element, such as :hover, :focus, :checked, and :nth-child(). Pseudo-elements represent a conceptual part of an element, such as ::before, ::after, and ::first-letter.

title: What is the difference between :nth-child() and :nth-of-type()?
answer: :nth-child() considers the element's position among all of its siblings. :nth-of-type() considers the position only among siblings of the same element type. This distinction is important when different element types are mixed within the same parent.

title: What are CSS transitions?
answer: CSS transitions allow a property value to change smoothly over a specified duration instead of changing immediately. Common properties include transition-property, transition-duration, transition-timing-function, and transition-delay.

title: What are CSS animations?
answer: CSS animations allow an element to change styles through a sequence of keyframes. They are defined using @keyframes and properties such as animation-name, animation-duration, animation-delay, animation-iteration-count, and animation-timing-function.

title: What is the difference between CSS transitions and animations?
answer: Transitions generally describe a smooth change between two states, usually triggered by a property change such as hover or focus. Animations can define multiple intermediate states using keyframes and can run automatically, repeat, reverse, or follow more complex timing patterns.

title: What are CSS transforms?
answer: CSS transforms allow elements to be translated, rotated, scaled, or skewed without changing the normal document flow in the same way that layout properties do. Common transform functions include translate(), rotate(), scale(), and skew().

title: Why are transform and opacity often preferred for smooth animations?
answer: Animations involving transform and opacity can often be handled efficiently by modern browser rendering pipelines without repeatedly recalculating layout. In contrast, frequently animating layout-affecting properties such as width, height, or top can cause additional layout and paint work. Actual performance should still be verified with browser profiling tools.

title: What is the difference between margin and padding?
answer: Margin creates space outside an element's border, while padding creates space between the element's content and its border. Padding contributes to the element's box size depending on the box-sizing value, while margin creates external spacing.

title: What is margin collapsing in CSS?
answer: Margin collapsing occurs when vertical margins of certain block-level elements combine into a single margin instead of adding together. Common cases include adjacent sibling margins and parent-child margins. Padding, borders, certain formatting contexts, and other layout conditions can prevent margin collapsing.

title: How can you prevent margin collapsing?
answer: Margin collapsing can be prevented by creating a different formatting context or introducing separation such as padding or border. Other approaches include using flexbox or grid layouts, where the relevant margin-collapsing behavior does not apply in the same way.

title: What is the difference between width: auto and width: 100%?
answer: width: auto allows the browser to determine the width based on the element's formatting context and available space. width: 100% explicitly sets the width to 100% of the containing block's relevant width, which can interact differently with padding and borders depending on box-sizing.

title: What are min-width, max-width, min-height, and max-height?
answer: These properties define constraints on an element's dimensions. min-width and min-height prevent an element from becoming smaller than the specified size, while max-width and max-height prevent it from becoming larger than the specified size.

title: What is the difference between height: 100% and height: 100vh?
answer: height: 100% depends on the containing block having a definite height. height: 100vh relates the height to the viewport's height. Modern viewport units such as svh, lvh, and dvh can provide more appropriate behavior on mobile browsers with dynamic browser UI.

title: What are viewport units in CSS?
answer: Viewport units represent dimensions relative to the browser viewport. Common units include vw, vh, vmin, and vmax. Modern CSS also provides dynamic, small, and large viewport units such as dvh, svh, and lvh.

title: What is the difference between rem and em units?
answer: rem is relative to the root element's font size. em is relative to the relevant element's font size and can therefore compound through nested elements. rem is often easier to reason about for consistent application-wide sizing.

title: What is the difference between px, %, em, rem, and vw?
answer: px is a CSS pixel unit. % is relative to a relevant containing value. em is relative to the relevant font size, rem is relative to the root font size, and vw is relative to the viewport width. The appropriate unit depends on the design and responsiveness requirements.

title: What are CSS custom properties?
answer: CSS custom properties are variables defined using names beginning with --. They can be referenced using the var() function. For example, --primary-color: blue; can be consumed using color: var(--primary-color).

title: What is the difference between CSS variables and Sass variables?
answer: CSS custom properties are native browser features and remain available at runtime, allowing them to participate in cascading and dynamic updates. Sass variables are processed during compilation and are replaced with their resulting values in the generated CSS. CSS custom properties are useful when values need to change dynamically in the browser.

title: What is the var() fallback mechanism in CSS?
answer: The var() function can specify a fallback value if the custom property is invalid or unavailable. For example, color: var(--primary-color, blue) uses blue when --primary-color cannot provide a valid value for that declaration.

title: What is the difference between CSS inheritance and the cascade?
answer: Inheritance determines whether a property value is passed from a parent element to its descendants. The cascade determines which applicable declaration wins when multiple declarations affect an element. Inheritance is one source of a value, while the cascade resolves competing declarations.

title: Which CSS properties are inherited by default?
answer: Many text-related properties such as color, font-family, and line-height commonly inherit by default. Many layout and box properties such as margin, padding, border, and width do not inherit by default.

title: What do the CSS values inherit, initial, unset, and revert mean?
answer: inherit explicitly uses the parent's computed value. initial resets the property to its specification-defined initial value. unset behaves like inherit for inherited properties and like initial for non-inherited properties. revert rolls the property back to a previous cascade origin or layer where applicable.

title: What is !important and why should it be used carefully?
answer: !important gives a declaration increased precedence within the cascade's importance rules. Excessive use makes styles difficult to override and maintain. It should generally be reserved for well-understood cases such as controlled utility classes or specific integration requirements.

title: What are CSS cascade layers?
answer: Cascade layers allow authors to explicitly organize CSS declarations into layers and control their precedence. They can make large stylesheets more predictable by establishing a deliberate ordering between reset styles, framework styles, components, utilities, and overrides without relying solely on specificity.

title: What is the difference between specificity and cascade layer order?
answer: Cascade layer ordering is considered before selector specificity within the relevant cascade steps. A declaration in a layer with higher precedence can win even when its selector has lower specificity than a declaration in another layer. This helps reduce the need for highly specific selectors.

title: What is a stacking context in CSS?
answer: A stacking context is an independent three-dimensional rendering context in which descendant elements are stacked relative to one another. Certain properties and conditions, such as positioned elements with applicable z-index, transforms, opacity less than 1, and other features, can create stacking contexts.

title: Why does z-index sometimes appear not to work?
answer: z-index operates within stacking contexts. An element with a high z-index inside one stacking context cannot necessarily appear above an element in another stacking context with a higher stacking level. Positioning, stacking-context creation, and DOM hierarchy should be inspected when debugging z-index issues.

title: What is the difference between overflow hidden, auto, scroll, and clip?
answer: hidden clips overflowing content and generally does not provide scrolling through that box. auto allows scrolling when needed. scroll provides a scrolling mechanism regardless of whether overflow currently requires it, subject to browser behavior. clip clips overflow without creating a scrolling mechanism.

title: What is the difference between overflow-wrap, word-break, and white-space?
answer: overflow-wrap controls whether long words or otherwise unbreakable strings may wrap. word-break controls how text can break between characters or words. white-space controls how whitespace and line wrapping are handled. They solve related but different text-layout problems.

title: What is the CSS position sticky behavior?
answer: An element with position: sticky participates in normal flow until its specified inset threshold, such as top: 0, is reached during scrolling. It then remains stuck within the boundaries of its containing scroll context until those boundaries are reached.

title: Why might position: sticky not work?
answer: Common causes include a missing inset such as top, an inappropriate ancestor with scrolling or overflow behavior, insufficient scrollable space, or layout conditions that prevent the sticky element from reaching its threshold. The containing block and scroll containers should be inspected carefully.

title: What is the difference between flex-basis, width, and flex-grow?
answer: flex-basis defines the initial main-size contribution of a flex item before free-space distribution. width defines a preferred width when applicable to the flex layout, while flex-grow determines how an item can receive positive free space relative to other flex items.

title: What do flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis mean?
answer: flex-grow controls how a flex item receives available positive space. flex-shrink controls how it participates when the flex container has insufficient space. flex-basis defines the item's initial main size before free-space distribution.

title: What does the flex shorthand property represent?
answer: The flex shorthand combines flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis. For example, flex: 1 is commonly used to allow an item to grow and shrink while using an automatically determined flex basis according to the shorthand rules.

title: What is the difference between gap, row-gap, and column-gap?
answer: gap is a shorthand for controlling both row and column spacing in supported layout contexts. row-gap controls spacing between rows, while column-gap controls spacing between columns. They are commonly used with Grid and Flexbox.

title: What is the difference between gap and margin for spacing layout items?
answer: gap creates consistent spacing between items in flex, grid, and related layouts without placing external margins on individual items. Margins belong to individual elements and can interact with the surrounding layout, including margin collapsing in some block layouts. Gap is often cleaner for spacing items within a layout container.

title: What are CSS Grid tracks?
answer: Grid tracks are the rows and columns created in a CSS Grid container. Row tracks are defined using grid-template-rows, while column tracks are defined using grid-template-columns. Track sizes can use units such as px, fr, percentages, and intrinsic sizing keywords.

title: What is the fr unit in CSS Grid?
answer: The fr unit represents a fraction of the available space in a grid container. For example, grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr distributes available space between two tracks in a 1-to-2 ratio after accounting for other sizing constraints.

title: What is the difference between auto-fit and auto-fill in CSS Grid?
answer: Both are commonly used with repeat() and responsive grid layouts. auto-fit collapses empty tracks so existing items can expand into available space, while auto-fill maintains the available track structure even when some tracks are empty. The difference becomes visible when there are fewer items than could fit.

title: What is the minmax() function in CSS Grid?
answer: minmax() defines a minimum and maximum size for a grid track. For example, minmax(200px, 1fr) ensures the track does not become smaller than 200 pixels while allowing it to grow and consume available space.

title: What is the repeat() function in CSS Grid?
answer: repeat() provides a concise way to define repeated grid tracks. For example, grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) creates three equal-width columns. It can also be combined with auto-fit, auto-fill, and minmax() for responsive layouts.

title: What is the difference between justify-items and justify-content in CSS Grid?
answer: justify-items controls how grid items are aligned within their individual grid areas along the inline axis. justify-content controls how the entire grid tracks are distributed within the grid container when there is extra space.

title: What is the difference between align-items and align-content in CSS Grid?
answer: align-items controls the alignment of grid items within their grid areas along the block axis. align-content controls how the entire grid tracks are distributed within the grid container when there is extra space.

title: What are CSS media queries?
answer: Media queries allow CSS rules to be applied conditionally based on characteristics of the user's environment, such as viewport width, orientation, resolution, or user preferences. They are commonly used to implement responsive and adaptive designs.

title: What is mobile-first responsive design?
answer: Mobile-first design starts with styles for smaller screens and progressively enhances the layout for larger screens using media queries. This approach encourages simpler base styles, focuses on essential content, and can make responsive CSS easier to maintain.

title: What is the difference between min-width and max-width media queries?
answer: A min-width media query applies styles when the viewport is at least the specified width. A max-width media query applies styles when the viewport is at most the specified width. Mobile-first designs commonly use progressively larger min-width breakpoints.

title: What are CSS container queries?
answer: Container queries allow styles to respond to the size or characteristics of a component's containing element rather than the viewport. This makes components more reusable because their layout can adapt based on the space available to the component.

title: What is the difference between media queries and container queries?
answer: Media queries typically respond to characteristics of the viewport or device environment. Container queries respond to the size or characteristics of a component's containing element. Container queries are particularly useful for reusable components that may appear in different layout contexts.

title: What is the CSS clamp() function?
answer: clamp() defines a value using a minimum, preferred, and maximum value. For example, font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem) allows the font size to scale responsively while remaining within defined limits.

title: What are min(), max(), and clamp() CSS functions used for?
answer: min() chooses the smallest valid value, max() chooses the largest valid value, and clamp() constrains a preferred value between a minimum and maximum. They are useful for creating responsive layouts without relying exclusively on multiple breakpoints.

title: What is the CSS calc() function?
answer: calc() allows CSS to perform calculations using compatible values and units. For example, width: calc(100% - 40px) can calculate a width based on the containing size while subtracting a fixed amount.

title: What is the difference between transform and position for moving an element?
answer: Positioning properties such as top, left, and related layout mechanisms can affect layout depending on the positioning mode. transform: translate() visually transforms an element without changing its normal layout position in the same way. Transforms are often useful for animations and visual movement.

title: What is will-change in CSS and when should it be used?
answer: will-change provides a hint to the browser that an element's property is expected to change. It can help browsers prepare for certain performance-sensitive changes, but excessive use can increase memory consumption and create performance problems. It should be used selectively and based on measured needs.

title: What is the difference between reflow and repaint?
answer: Reflow, also called layout, occurs when the browser recalculates the geometry and positions of elements. Repaint occurs when visual appearance changes without necessarily requiring layout recalculation. Layout changes can be more expensive because they may trigger additional rendering work for affected content.

title: Which CSS properties commonly trigger layout changes?
answer: Properties related to geometry and layout, such as width, height, margin, padding, top, and left in relevant positioning contexts, can trigger layout recalculation when changed. The actual rendering cost depends on the surrounding document and browser implementation.

title: What is the prefers-reduced-motion media feature?
answer: prefers-reduced-motion allows a website to detect when a user has requested reduced motion through their operating-system or browser accessibility settings. Developers can reduce or disable non-essential animations and transitions for users who prefer less motion.

title: What is prefers-color-scheme in CSS?
answer: prefers-color-scheme allows CSS to respond to the user's preferred light or dark color scheme. For example, @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) can define styles appropriate for dark mode.

title: What is the difference between inline-flex and flex?
answer: display: flex makes the element a block-level flex container, while display: inline-flex makes it an inline-level flex container. In both cases, the children participate in flex layout.

title: What is flex-direction in CSS?
answer: flex-direction defines the main axis of a flex container. Common values are row, row-reverse, column, and column-reverse.

title: What is flex-wrap and why is it useful?
answer: flex-wrap controls whether flex items remain on one line or wrap onto multiple lines. The values include nowrap, wrap, and wrap-reverse. It is useful for creating responsive layouts when there is insufficient space for all items on one line.

title: What is align-self in Flexbox?
answer: align-self allows an individual flex item to override the container's align-items value. It controls the item's alignment along the cross axis.

title: What is the order property in Flexbox?
answer: The order property controls the visual ordering of flex and grid items without changing their order in the HTML source. The default value is 0. It should be used carefully because changing visual order can create accessibility and keyboard-navigation issues if it conflicts with the logical document order.

title: What is the difference between flex-start and start?
answer: flex-start is specific to flex layout's main or cross axis depending on the property. Logical values such as start and end are based more directly on the writing mode and text direction. Logical alignment values can be useful when supporting internationalized layouts.

title: What is CSS logical property support?
answer: Logical properties allow styles to adapt to writing direction and writing mode. Examples include margin-inline, padding-block, inset-inline-start, and border-block-end. They are useful for internationalization because they avoid assuming a fixed left-to-right layout.

title: What is the difference between margin-left and margin-inline-start?
answer: margin-left always refers to the physical left side. margin-inline-start refers to the start side of the inline axis, which changes according to the document's writing direction. Logical properties are preferable when supporting multiple writing directions.

title: What is CSS writing-mode?
answer: writing-mode controls whether text and layout flow horizontally or vertically. Values such as horizontal-tb, vertical-rl, and vertical-lr allow CSS to support different writing systems and layout directions.

title: What is the difference between left/right and inline-start/inline-end?
answer: left and right are physical directions. inline-start and inline-end are logical directions determined by writing mode and text direction. Logical properties make layouts easier to adapt to RTL and vertical writing modes.

title: What is object-fit in CSS?
answer: object-fit controls how replaced content such as an image or video fits inside its specified dimensions. Common values include cover, contain, fill, none, and scale-down.

title: What is the difference between object-fit: cover and contain?
answer: cover scales the replaced content so the container is completely covered, potentially cropping part of the content. contain scales the content so the entire content remains visible, potentially leaving empty space inside the container.

title: What is object-position?
answer: object-position controls the alignment of replaced content such as an image when it does not completely fill its content box. It is commonly combined with object-fit: cover to control which part of an image remains visible.

title: What is aspect-ratio in CSS?
answer: The aspect-ratio property defines a preferred width-to-height ratio for an element's box. For example, aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 can maintain a 16:9 shape while the element's size changes responsively.

title: How does aspect-ratio help responsive image and card layouts?
answer: aspect-ratio allows a component to maintain a consistent shape without manually calculating its height. It is useful for responsive images, video containers, cards, thumbnails, and media grids.

title: What is the CSS isolation property?
answer: The isolation property controls whether an element creates a new stacking context. For example, isolation: isolate can be useful when preventing blending or stacking behavior from interacting with elements outside a component.

title: What is mix-blend-mode in CSS?
answer: mix-blend-mode controls how an element's content blends with the content behind it. It provides effects similar to image-editing blend modes, such as multiply or screen, and should be used carefully because it can affect readability and rendering performance.

title: What is background-blend-mode?
answer: background-blend-mode controls how an element's background images and background colors blend with each other. It is useful for creating visual effects without requiring additional image-editing assets.

title: What is the difference between linear-gradient and radial-gradient?
answer: linear-gradient() creates a gradient along a straight line. radial-gradient() creates a gradient radiating outward from a point or shape. Both can be used as CSS background images.

title: Can CSS gradients be used as background images?
answer: Yes. CSS gradients such as linear-gradient(), radial-gradient(), and conic-gradient() generate images that can be used with the background-image property. They can reduce the need for separate image assets.

title: What is a conic gradient in CSS?
answer: conic-gradient() creates a gradient that rotates around a center point. It is useful for visualizations such as pie-chart-like effects, color wheels, and circular progress indicators.

title: What is the difference between background-size: cover and contain?
answer: cover scales the background image so the entire background area is covered, potentially cropping the image. contain scales the image so the entire image fits inside the background area, potentially leaving empty space.

title: What is background-position used for?
answer: background-position controls where a background image is positioned within its background positioning area. Values such as center, top, right, and percentage or length values can be used to control the visible portion of the image.

title: What is the difference between background and img elements?
answer: An <img> element represents an image as content and supports semantics such as alternative text. A CSS background image is generally presentation and decoration. Important content images should normally use <img> with appropriate alternative text rather than CSS backgrounds.

title: What is CSS filter?
answer: The filter property applies graphical effects such as blur, brightness, contrast, grayscale, hue rotation, inversion, opacity, and saturation. Filters can be applied to images and other rendered elements.

title: What is the difference between opacity and filter: opacity()?
answer: The opacity property controls the transparency of the entire element and its descendants as a rendered group. filter: opacity() applies opacity as a filter effect. Although their visual result can be similar, they participate differently in rendering and can have different compositing behavior.

title: What is CSS backdrop-filter?
answer: backdrop-filter applies graphical effects to the content behind an element, such as blur or saturation. It is commonly used to create glass-like interfaces. The element generally needs appropriate transparency for the backdrop effect to be visible.

title: What are CSS shadows?
answer: CSS provides box-shadow for element boxes and text-shadow for text. Shadows can specify horizontal and vertical offsets, blur radius, spread for box shadows, and color.

title: What is the difference between box-shadow and drop-shadow?
answer: box-shadow is based on the element's box geometry. filter: drop-shadow() follows the rendered alpha shape of the element, which can make it more suitable for transparent images or irregular shapes.

title: What is the CSS clip-path property?
answer: clip-path defines a clipping region that determines which portion of an element is visible. Shapes such as circles, ellipses, polygons, and custom paths can be used to create non-rectangular visual shapes.

title: What is the difference between clip-path and border-radius?
answer: border-radius rounds the corners of an element's box. clip-path can create much more complex clipping shapes such as polygons and circles. Clip paths provide greater geometric flexibility.

title: What is CSS mask-image?
answer: mask-image uses an image, gradient, or other mask source to control which parts of an element are visible. Masking can create complex transparency and visual effects without modifying the underlying HTML.

title: What is the difference between visibility and opacity for accessibility?
answer: visibility: hidden generally removes the element from the accessibility tree and makes it unavailable to interaction. opacity: 0 makes the element transparent but does not necessarily remove it from accessibility or interaction. Therefore, opacity should not be assumed to hide an element semantically.

title: What is pointer-events in CSS?
answer: The pointer-events property controls whether an element can be the target of pointer interactions. For example, pointer-events: none allows pointer events to pass through an element to content underneath. It should not be used as a replacement for proper keyboard accessibility.

title: What is the caret-color property?
answer: caret-color controls the color of the text insertion caret in editable elements such as text inputs and textareas. It can be useful when customizing form controls while maintaining a visible editing indicator.

title: What is accent-color in CSS?
answer: accent-color allows authors to customize the accent color used by certain form controls, such as checkboxes, radio buttons, range inputs, and progress elements, while retaining the browser's native control behavior.

title: What is appearance in CSS?
answer: The appearance property controls whether an element uses the browser's native UI styling or a more author-controlled appearance. It is commonly used when customizing native form controls, although browser behavior and accessibility should be considered carefully.

title: What is the CSS accent-color property useful for in design systems?
answer: accent-color can provide a consistent brand or theme color for supported native form controls without replacing their native semantics and interaction behavior. This can reduce the amount of custom CSS and JavaScript required for simple controls.

title: What is the difference between CSS reset and CSS normalize?
answer: A CSS reset generally removes or standardizes many browser default styles to provide a clean starting point. Normalize-style approaches preserve useful browser defaults while making rendering more consistent across browsers. The choice depends on the project's design and browser-support strategy.

title: Why is box-sizing: border-box commonly applied globally?
answer: box-sizing: border-box makes declared dimensions include padding and borders, which often makes layout calculations more predictable. Applying it consistently across elements can reduce unexpected size calculations in responsive layouts.

title: What is the CSS universal selector?
answer: The universal selector is written as * and matches all elements within the relevant scope. It is commonly used in resets and global rules, but broad selectors should be used thoughtfully to avoid unnecessary style matching and unintended inheritance or overrides.

title: What is the difference between child and descendant selectors?
answer: The descendant selector, represented by a space such as .card p, matches paragraphs at any descendant level. The child selector, represented by > such as .card > p, matches only direct children of the selected parent.

title: What is the difference between adjacent sibling and general sibling selectors?
answer: The adjacent sibling selector + matches the immediately following sibling. The general sibling selector ~ matches subsequent siblings that share the same parent. For example, h2 + p targets only the first paragraph immediately after an h2, while h2 ~ p can target later paragraphs as well.

title: What is the :is() pseudo-class?
answer: :is() groups multiple selectors into a single selector expression. For example, :is(h1, h2, h3) can target all three heading levels. It can reduce repetitive selectors and simplify complex stylesheets.

title: What is the difference between :is() and :where()?
answer: Both :is() and :where() group selectors, but their specificity differs. The specificity of :is() is based on the most specific selector in its argument list, while :where() has zero specificity. This makes :where() useful for creating styles that are easy to override.

title: What is the :has() pseudo-class?
answer: :has() is a relational pseudo-class that allows a selector to match an element based on the presence of matching descendants or related elements. For example, .card:has(img) selects cards that contain an image. It enables patterns that previously required JavaScript for many use cases.

title: Why is :has() sometimes called a parent selector?
answer: :has() can select an element based on what it contains, which enables patterns commonly associated with parent selection. For example, .form-group:has(input:invalid) can style a form group when it contains an invalid input. More precisely, it is a relational pseudo-class rather than simply a parent selector.

title: What is the :not() pseudo-class?
answer: :not() matches elements that do not match the selector provided inside it. For example, button:not(.primary) selects buttons that do not have the primary class. It is useful for expressing exclusion rules.

title: What is the difference between :first-child and :first-of-type?
answer: :first-child matches an element only if it is the first child of its parent, regardless of sibling type. :first-of-type matches an element if it is the first sibling of its specific element type.

title: How would you design a scalable CSS architecture for a large React application?
answer: I would establish clear conventions for component styles, design tokens, spacing, typography, responsive breakpoints, and reusable utilities. I would minimize global selectors, control cascade and specificity, use CSS Modules or another appropriate scoping strategy when useful, and organize styles around components rather than pages. For a large application, I would also consider CSS custom properties, cascade layers, accessibility, theming, and performance.

title: What is the difference between CSS Grid's auto-placement and explicit placement?
answer: Auto-placement allows the browser to position grid items according to the grid's auto-placement algorithm. Explicit placement uses properties such as grid-column and grid-row to specify where an item should be placed. Explicit placement provides more precise control over complex layouts.

title: What are grid-column and grid-row properties?
answer: grid-column controls the column lines between which a grid item is placed, while grid-row controls its row lines. They can specify start and end positions, such as grid-column: 1 / 3.

title: What is grid-template-areas?
answer: grid-template-areas allows developers to define named areas of a CSS Grid using a visual string representation. Individual grid items can then use grid-area to assign themselves to those named areas. It can make page-level layouts easier to understand.

title: How do you create a responsive three-column layout using CSS Grid?
answer: A simple approach is display: grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr). For responsiveness, this can be combined with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)), allowing the number of columns to adapt automatically based on available space.

title: What is the difference between explicit and implicit grid tracks?
answer: Explicit grid tracks are created using properties such as grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. Implicit tracks are automatically created by the browser when items are placed outside the explicitly defined grid. Their sizing can be controlled with grid-auto-columns and grid-auto-rows.

title: What is grid-auto-flow?
answer: grid-auto-flow controls how automatically placed grid items are inserted into the grid. Values include row, column, and dense. The dense option can attempt to fill earlier gaps, but it may change the visual order of items.

title: What is the difference between align-content, justify-content, and place-content?
answer: align-content controls distribution along the block or cross axis, while justify-content controls distribution along the inline or main axis depending on the layout. place-content is a shorthand for setting both align-content and justify-content.

title: What is place-items in CSS?
answer: place-items is a shorthand for align-items and justify-items. It is particularly useful with CSS Grid when the same alignment value should be applied along both axes.

title: What is place-self in CSS?
answer: place-self is a shorthand for align-self and justify-self. It allows an individual grid item to control its alignment along both axes.

title: What is the difference between justify-self and justify-items?
answer: justify-items sets the default inline-axis alignment for items within a grid container. justify-self controls the alignment of an individual grid item and can override the container's default.

title: How do you center an element horizontally and vertically using Flexbox?
answer: Set the parent to display: flex and use justify-content: center and align-items: center. For example, .container { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }.

title: How do you center an element using CSS Grid?
answer: One simple approach is display: grid with place-items: center. This centers the grid item along both axes when the grid container has available space.

title: What is the difference between text-align and justify-content?
answer: text-align controls the inline alignment of text and inline-level content within a block or text container. justify-content controls the distribution of flex or grid content within a layout container. They solve different alignment problems.

title: What is line-height and why is it important?
answer: line-height controls the height of a line box and therefore affects vertical spacing between lines of text. Appropriate line height improves readability, especially for paragraphs and long-form content. Unitless values are often useful because they scale naturally with the element's font size.

title: What is the difference between font-size and line-height?
answer: font-size controls the size of the text glyphs, while line-height controls the vertical space allocated to each line of text. A larger line height can improve readability without increasing the actual font size.

title: What is the difference between font-weight values 400 and 700?
answer: In the common CSS font-weight scale, 400 corresponds to normal weight and 700 corresponds to bold weight. The actual visual result depends on the font and whether the requested weight is available.

title: What are variable fonts in CSS?
answer: Variable fonts contain a range of font variations within a single font file. CSS can control axes such as weight, width, and slant, potentially reducing the need to load multiple static font files. They can provide flexible typography and potentially improve asset management.

title: What is the @font-face rule?
answer: @font-face allows a web page to define a custom font resource that the browser can download and use. It can specify the font family, source files, weight, style, display behavior, and other descriptors.

title: What is font-display in @font-face?
answer: font-display controls how text is rendered while a web font is loading. Values such as swap, block, fallback, and optional provide different trade-offs between immediate text rendering and waiting for the custom font.

title: What is the difference between serif and sans-serif fonts?
answer: Serif fonts have decorative strokes at the ends of characters, while sans-serif fonts do not. The choice affects visual style, readability, and brand identity. CSS can specify generic families such as serif and sans-serif as fallbacks.

title: What is text-overflow: ellipsis?
answer: text-overflow: ellipsis displays an ellipsis when text overflows its box and is clipped. A common single-line implementation combines it with overflow: hidden and white-space: nowrap.

title: How do you create a multi-line text ellipsis using modern CSS?
answer: Multi-line truncation can be implemented using techniques based on line clamping, commonly with -webkit-line-clamp together with the required display and overflow settings. Browser support and exact behavior should be checked for the application's target browsers.

title: What is white-space: nowrap?
answer: white-space: nowrap prevents normal line wrapping within the element. It is often combined with overflow: hidden and text-overflow: ellipsis to create single-line truncated text.

title: What is word-spacing and letter-spacing?
answer: word-spacing controls additional spacing between words, while letter-spacing controls spacing between individual characters. They can be useful for typography adjustments but should be used carefully to maintain readability.

title: What is text-transform in CSS?
answer: text-transform controls the capitalization presentation of text. Common values include uppercase, lowercase, capitalize, and none. It changes visual presentation rather than the underlying text content.

title: What is text-decoration in CSS?
answer: text-decoration controls decorations such as underline, overline, and line-through. Related properties allow control over decoration color, style, thickness, and offset.

title: What is the difference between visibility and display in CSS?
answer: display determines how an element participates in layout and can remove it from layout with display: none. visibility controls whether the element is visually rendered while generally preserving its layout space when hidden.

title: What is the difference between relative and absolute units in CSS?
answer: Absolute units represent fixed physical or CSS dimensions, with px being the most common web unit. Relative units depend on another measurement, such as %, em, rem, vw, and vh. Relative units are especially useful for responsive layouts.

title: What is the difference between transform: scale() and changing width or height?
answer: transform: scale() visually scales an element without changing its normal layout dimensions. Changing width or height changes layout geometry and can trigger layout recalculation for affected content. Transforms are therefore commonly preferred for visual scaling animations.

title: What is transform-origin?
answer: transform-origin defines the point around which a transform is applied. The default is generally the center of the element's box. Changing it is useful for effects such as rotating an element around a corner or scaling from a specific point.

title: What is perspective in CSS 3D transforms?
answer: perspective establishes the distance between the viewer and the z=0 plane, creating a sense of depth for 3D-transformed elements. It can be applied to a parent container or used through the perspective() transform function.

title: What is transform-style: preserve-3d?
answer: transform-style: preserve-3d allows an element's children to maintain their three-dimensional positioning rather than being flattened into the parent's plane. It is commonly used when building nested 3D transformations.

title: What is backface-visibility?
answer: backface-visibility controls whether the back side of a transformed element is visible when the element is rotated in 3D space. Setting it to hidden is commonly used for card-flip animations.

title: What is the CSS transition-timing-function property?
answer: transition-timing-function controls the rate at which an animated transition progresses over time. Common values include ease, linear, ease-in, ease-out, and ease-in-out. Custom cubic-bezier functions can provide more precise timing.

title: What is cubic-bezier() in CSS animations?
answer: cubic-bezier() defines a custom easing curve for transitions and animations. It uses four control-point values to determine how the animation progresses between its starting and ending states.

title: What is animation-fill-mode?
answer: animation-fill-mode determines how an animated element's styles apply before and after the animation. Values include none, forwards, backwards, and both. For example, forwards keeps the styles from the final keyframe after the animation finishes.

title: What is animation-direction?
answer: animation-direction controls the direction in which an animation plays. Values include normal, reverse, alternate, and alternate-reverse. Alternate modes allow an animation to reverse direction on successive iterations.

title: How do you pause and resume a CSS animation?
answer: Use the animation-play-state property. Setting it to paused pauses the animation, while running resumes it. JavaScript can toggle a CSS class that changes this property when user interaction is required.

title: What is the difference between transition-duration and animation-duration?
answer: transition-duration specifies how long a transition between property values takes. animation-duration specifies how long one iteration of a keyframe animation takes. Transitions and animations have different triggering and configuration models.

title: What is CSS scroll-behavior?
answer: scroll-behavior controls whether scrolling caused by navigation or CSSOM scrolling behaves instantly or smoothly. For example, scroll-behavior: smooth can provide smooth scrolling for supported programmatic and fragment navigation operations.

title: What is scroll-snap-type in CSS?
answer: scroll-snap-type enables scroll snapping within a scroll container. It defines the axis and strictness of snapping, allowing interfaces such as carousels and paginated horizontal sections to settle at defined snap positions.

title: What are scroll-snap-align and scroll-snap-stop?
answer: scroll-snap-align defines the snap position of an individual child within a scroll container. scroll-snap-stop can require scrolling to stop at a snap point rather than passing over it during certain scroll interactions.

title: What is overscroll-behavior in CSS?
answer: overscroll-behavior controls what happens when a scroll container reaches the boundary of its scrollable area. It can prevent scroll chaining to ancestor containers and can also help suppress certain browser overscroll effects.

title: What is touch-action in CSS?
answer: touch-action controls which touch and pointer gestures the browser may handle on an element. It is useful for custom touch interactions and pointer-event applications because it allows developers to declare which gestures should remain available to the browser.

title: How would you optimize CSS performance in a large React application?
answer: I would remove unused CSS, reduce unnecessary selector complexity, avoid excessive global styles, split styles where appropriate, optimize critical rendering paths, minimize expensive animations, use efficient component-level styling, and avoid unnecessary DOM complexity.
