I would also inspect generated CSS bundle sizes and use browser performance tools to identify actual rendering bottlenecks.

title: What is critical CSS?
answer: Critical CSS is the subset of styles required to render the initially visible portion of a page. Delivering critical styles early can reduce render-blocking work and improve perceived loading performance. Non-critical styles can be loaded separately when appropriate.

title: What is CSS containment?
answer: CSS containment allows developers to tell the browser that certain aspects of an element's rendering or layout can be treated as independent from the rest of the document. Properties such as contain can help limit the scope of layout, paint, or size calculations and may improve performance in appropriate component architectures.

title: What is content-visibility in CSS?
answer: content-visibility allows the browser to skip certain rendering work for content that does not need to be immediately rendered. For example, content-visibility: auto can help improve performance for large pages containing content outside the current viewport.

title: What is contain-intrinsic-size?
answer: contain-intrinsic-size provides a placeholder intrinsic size for an element when rendering work is skipped through features such as content visibility or size containment. This can help the browser reserve appropriate space and reduce unexpected layout shifts.

title: What is the difference between CSS transitions, animations, and JavaScript animations?
answer: CSS transitions handle changes between states, CSS animations provide keyframe-based sequences, and JavaScript animations provide programmatic control over timing, state, and complex interaction logic. CSS is often preferred for straightforward visual effects, while JavaScript is useful when animation behavior depends heavily on application state or complex calculations.

title: What is the difference between .on() and .one() in jQuery?
answer: .on() attaches an event handler that can execute multiple times. .one() attaches a handler that is automatically removed after it executes once. Use .one() when an action should happen only on the first occurrence of an event.

title: What is the difference between .off() and .unbind() in jQuery?
answer: .off() is the modern API for removing event handlers registered with .on(). .unbind() is an older API that has been deprecated and removed from modern jQuery usage. New code should use .off().

title: What is the difference between .click() and .on('click') in jQuery?
answer: .click() is a shorthand event API, while .on('click') is the more flexible event API. The .on() method supports direct and delegated event handling, event namespaces, and a consistent event-registration model. For modern jQuery code, .on() is generally preferred.

title: What is event.preventDefault() in jQuery?
answer: event.preventDefault() prevents the browser's default action for an event. For example, it can prevent a link from navigating or prevent a form submission while custom JavaScript validation or processing is performed.

title: What is the difference between preventDefault() and stopPropagation()?
answer: preventDefault() prevents the browser's default action, while stopPropagation() prevents the event from continuing through the propagation path. They solve different problems and can be used independently or together when necessary.

title: What does event.stopImmediatePropagation() do?
answer: stopImmediatePropagation() prevents the event from propagating and also prevents other handlers registered on the same element from executing after the current handler. It should be used carefully because it can interfere with unrelated event handlers.

title: What is the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget in jQuery?
answer: event.target refers to the element where the event originated. event.currentTarget refers to the element whose handler is currently being executed. In delegated events, these values can be different because the handler is attached to an ancestor while the event originates from a descendant.

title: How do you dynamically add elements and attach events in jQuery?
answer: Use event delegation when elements may be created dynamically. For example, $('#list').on('click', '.item', handler) attaches one handler to the list and handles clicks from current and future elements matching .item.

title: What is the difference between .append(), .prepend(), .before(), and .after()?
answer: .append() inserts content at the end of an element's children. .prepend() inserts it at the beginning. .before() inserts content immediately before the selected element, while .after() inserts it immediately after the selected element.

title: What is the difference between .append() and .appendTo()?
answer: .append() is called on the target parent and receives the content to insert, while .appendTo() is called on the content and receives the target parent. For example, $('#child').appendTo('#parent') is conceptually equivalent to $('#parent').append($('#child')).

title: What is the difference between .remove(), .empty(), and .detach()?
answer: .remove() removes the selected elements and their associated jQuery data and event handlers. .empty() removes the child nodes from the selected elements. .detach() removes the elements while preserving their jQuery-associated data and event handlers, making it useful when elements may be reinserted.

title: What is the difference between .html() and .text()?
answer: .html() gets or sets HTML markup inside an element. .text() gets or sets text content and treats the supplied value as text rather than HTML. When displaying untrusted user input, using .text() is generally safer because it does not interpret the input as HTML.

title: What is the difference between .attr() and .prop()?
answer: .attr() works with HTML attributes, while .prop() accesses DOM properties. For example, the current checked state of a checkbox should generally be read using .prop('checked'), while the original HTML attribute can be accessed using .attr('checked').

title: Why should prop() be used instead of attr() for checkbox state?
answer: The checked attribute represents the markup's initial state, while the DOM's checked property represents the current state. Therefore, $('#check').prop('checked') is the appropriate way to determine whether a checkbox is currently checked.

title: What is the difference between .val(), .text(), and .html()?
answer: .val() gets or sets the value of form controls. .text() gets or sets text content. .html() gets or sets HTML markup. The appropriate method depends on whether the data represents a form value, plain text, or HTML.

title: What is the difference between .addClass(), .removeClass(), .toggleClass(), and .hasClass()?
answer: .addClass() adds classes, .removeClass() removes classes, .toggleClass() adds or removes classes depending on their current state, and .hasClass() checks whether at least one selected element has a specified class.

title: How do you get the width and height of an element using jQuery?
answer: jQuery provides methods such as .width(), .height(), .innerWidth(), .innerHeight(), .outerWidth(), and .outerHeight(). These methods differ in whether padding, borders, and margins are included.

title: What is the difference between width(), innerWidth(), and outerWidth()?
answer: width() generally returns the content width. innerWidth() includes padding, while outerWidth() includes padding and borders. With the optional margin argument, outerWidth(true) can also include margins.

title: What is the difference between .offset() and .position()?
answer: .offset() returns an element's position relative to the document. .position() returns its position relative to its offset parent. These methods are useful for different positioning and layout calculations.

title: What are scrollTop() and scrollLeft() used for?
answer: .scrollTop() gets or sets the vertical scroll position, while .scrollLeft() gets or sets the horizontal scroll position. They can be used to implement features such as scroll-to-top buttons or synchronized scrolling.

title: What is the difference between each() and map() in jQuery?
answer: .each() iterates over a jQuery collection and is commonly used for side effects. .map() transforms each item into a new value and returns a jQuery collection containing the mapped results. The two methods serve different purposes.

title: What is the difference between $.each() and $(selector).each()?
answer: $(selector).each() iterates over the elements in a jQuery collection. $.each() is a utility method that can iterate over arrays, array-like objects, and other supported collections. The static utility is not limited to jQuery element collections.

title: What does return false mean inside a jQuery event handler?
answer: Returning false from a jQuery event handler is a shorthand that prevents the default action and stops event propagation. However, explicit calls to event.preventDefault() and event.stopPropagation() are often clearer because they communicate the intended behavior separately.

title: What is jQuery chaining?
answer: jQuery chaining allows multiple methods to be called sequentially on the same jQuery collection. For example, $('.item').addClass('active').hide().fadeIn() chains several operations. Many jQuery methods return the jQuery object to support this pattern.

title: What is the end() method in jQuery?
answer: The .end() method returns the previous jQuery collection in the chain. It is useful after traversal operations such as .find() when you want to return to the previous selection and continue chaining.

title: What is the difference between find() and children()?
answer: .find() searches through all descendant levels for elements matching a selector. .children() considers only immediate child elements. Therefore, .find() provides deeper traversal than .children().

title: What is the difference between parent(), parents(), and closest()?
answer: .parent() returns the immediate parent. .parents() searches through ancestors. .closest() searches the element itself and then ancestors until it finds the first element matching the selector. .closest() is particularly useful for event delegation.

title: What is the difference between siblings(), next(), and prev()?
answer: .siblings() returns sibling elements. .next() returns the immediately following sibling, while .prev() returns the immediately preceding sibling. Selector arguments can be used to filter the results.

title: What is the difference between filter(), not(), and has()?
answer: .filter() keeps elements that match a selector or condition. .not() removes elements that match. .has() keeps elements that contain at least one matching descendant. These methods are useful for refining jQuery collections.

title: What is the difference between eq(), first(), and last()?
answer: .eq(index) selects an element at a specific zero-based index. .first() selects the first element, while .last() selects the final element in the current jQuery collection.

title: What is the difference between :first and :first-child in jQuery?
answer: :first is a jQuery selector that selects the first element in the matched result set. :first-child is a CSS structural pseudo-class that selects an element only when it is the first child of its parent. They represent different concepts.

title: What is the difference between CSS selectors and jQuery-specific selectors?
answer: jQuery supports standard CSS selectors and historically provided additional selector extensions. Modern code should prefer standard CSS selectors when possible because browsers can optimize them through native selector APIs. jQuery-specific selectors may require jQuery's selector engine.

title: What is jQuery AJAX?
answer: jQuery AJAX APIs allow JavaScript to communicate with a server asynchronously without requiring a full page reload. Common APIs include $.ajax(), $.get(), and $.post(). They can handle HTTP requests, responses, errors, and callbacks or promise-like completion handling.

title: What is the difference between $.ajax(), $.get(), and $.post()?
answer: $.ajax() provides the most configuration options, including HTTP method, headers, data, timeout, and response handling. $.get() is a convenience method for GET requests, while $.post() is a convenience method for POST requests.

title: What are the important options in $.ajax()?
answer: Common options include url, method or type, data, dataType, contentType, headers, timeout, beforeSend, success, error, and complete. The exact options used depend on the API and application requirements.

title: What is the difference between dataType and contentType in jQuery AJAX?
answer: dataType tells jQuery what type of response the client expects to receive and process. contentType describes the type of data being sent in the request body. For example, sending JSON commonly uses contentType: 'application/json', while dataType: 'json' indicates that the response should be interpreted as JSON.

title: How do you handle AJAX errors in jQuery?
answer: Errors can be handled using the error callback or the promise-like methods such as .fail(). A robust implementation should inspect the HTTP status, response information, and application-specific error payload and provide an appropriate user-facing message.

title: What are .done(), .fail(), and .always() in jQuery AJAX?
answer: .done() handles successful completion, .fail() handles failed completion, and .always() runs regardless of success or failure. They provide a cleaner way to attach completion handlers to jQuery's Deferred-based asynchronous operations.

title: What is $.when() in jQuery?
answer: $.when() provides a way to coordinate multiple jQuery Deferred or promise-like objects. It can be used when an operation should continue after multiple asynchronous operations have completed. For modern JavaScript applications, native Promise.all() is often preferred when working with native promises.

title: What is a jQuery Deferred object?
answer: A jQuery Deferred is an object used to manage the completion of asynchronous operations and expose callback registration through methods such as done(), fail(), and always(). jQuery AJAX operations use this Deferred/promise-like model.

title: What is $.proxy() in jQuery?
answer: $.proxy() was historically used to control the this value when invoking a function. It has been deprecated in modern jQuery versions. Native JavaScript Function.prototype.bind() is the preferred approach for binding function context.

title: What is the purpose of jQuery.ready?
answer: jQuery's ready mechanism runs code when the DOM is ready to be safely manipulated. A common form is $(function() { ... }). It avoids relying on the exact timing of script placement when initialization requires the DOM to have been parsed.

title: What is the difference between DOMContentLoaded and jQuery ready?
answer: DOMContentLoaded is a native browser event fired when the HTML document has been parsed and the DOM is ready. jQuery's ready mechanism provides a convenient abstraction around DOM readiness and handles registration details for jQuery applications. In modern applications, native DOMContentLoaded is also available when jQuery is unnecessary.

title: What are jQuery 4's major modernization goals?
answer: jQuery 4 focuses on modernizing the library, removing long-deprecated APIs and legacy browser support, and aligning the project more closely with current web-platform behavior. When upgrading a project, deprecated APIs and browser assumptions should be reviewed carefully against the specific jQuery 4 release and migration guidance.

title: What should you check before upgrading a project from jQuery 3 to jQuery 4?
answer: I would audit deprecated APIs, third-party plugins, event handling, AJAX usage, browser support requirements, selector usage, and custom extensions to jQuery internals. I would also run the official migration tooling where appropriate, execute the application's automated tests, and test critical user flows in supported browsers.

title: Why can old jQuery plugins break after upgrading to jQuery 4?
answer: Older plugins may depend on APIs that have been deprecated or removed, legacy browser behavior, undocumented jQuery internals, or assumptions about DOM and event behavior. Plugin compatibility should therefore be verified before upgrading a production application.

title: What is the jQuery Migrate plugin and why is it useful during upgrades?
answer: jQuery Migrate helps identify compatibility problems when upgrading between jQuery versions by restoring or warning about certain deprecated behaviors. It can be useful during migration because it helps developers locate code that needs to be updated before removing compatibility support.

title: Should jQuery 4 be used for every modern web application?
answer: No. The choice depends on the application. jQuery can still be useful for maintaining an existing jQuery-based application or integrating with legacy plugins. For a new application, native DOM APIs and modern frameworks may provide the required functionality without adding jQuery as a dependency.

title: How would you optimize a large jQuery application?
answer: I would minimize unnecessary DOM queries, cache frequently used selections, use event delegation for dynamic collections, batch DOM updates, avoid repeated layout reads and writes, reduce unnecessary animations, remove unused plugins, optimize AJAX calls, and clean up event handlers when components are destroyed. I would verify improvements using browser profiling tools rather than optimizing based only on assumptions.

title: How would you migrate a large jQuery application to React?
answer: I would avoid rewriting the entire application at once. I would identify clear feature boundaries, gradually introduce React into isolated sections, establish communication between React and existing jQuery code, migrate state and event handling incrementally, and remove jQuery dependencies as each area is converted. Automated tests and incremental releases would reduce migration risk.

title: How can you reduce unnecessary DOM queries in jQuery?
answer: Cache frequently used jQuery selections instead of repeatedly querying the DOM. For example, store const $list = $('#userList') and reuse it rather than calling $('#userList') multiple times. This reduces selector processing and improves readability.

title: Why should you cache jQuery selectors?
answer: Repeatedly executing the same selector can cause unnecessary DOM traversal and selector processing. Caching a jQuery collection allows the application to reuse the existing selection, which can improve performance when the same elements are accessed frequently.

title: How can you optimize jQuery selectors?
answer: Use simple and specific selectors, scope searches to a known container, avoid unnecessarily complex selectors, and cache frequently used results. For example, $container.find('.item') can be preferable to repeatedly searching the entire document for the same elements.

title: Is $('#id') faster than $('.class') in jQuery?
answer: An ID selector can often be highly efficient because browsers provide optimized native lookup mechanisms for IDs. However, modern selector engines and browsers are highly optimized, so the practical difference may be small. The more important optimization is avoiding unnecessary repeated DOM queries and using appropriately scoped selectors.

title: How can you avoid repeated DOM traversal in jQuery?
answer: Cache parent containers and frequently accessed collections, traverse only when necessary, and reuse references. Methods such as find(), children(), and closest() should be used with an appropriately scoped starting element rather than repeatedly searching the entire document.

title: What is DOM manipulation and why can it be expensive?
answer: DOM manipulation means adding, removing, moving, or changing elements and their properties. Frequent changes can cause the browser to recalculate style, layout, paint, and compositing work. Large numbers of individual DOM updates can therefore become expensive.

title: How can you reduce DOM manipulation in jQuery?
answer: Batch updates, construct content before inserting it, modify classes instead of repeatedly changing individual styles, minimize unnecessary reads and writes, and update the DOM only when the UI actually needs to change. For large lists, generate content efficiently before inserting it.

title: What is document fragment and how can it improve jQuery performance?
answer: A document fragment is an in-memory container that can hold DOM nodes before they are inserted into the document. Building multiple elements in a fragment and inserting the fragment once can reduce repeated DOM updates. jQuery methods can also internally optimize certain multi-element operations.

title: How would you efficiently render 10,000 rows using jQuery?
answer: I would avoid inserting each row individually into the live DOM. I would generate the markup in memory, preferably in batches, and perform fewer DOM insertions. For very large datasets, I would also consider pagination, virtualization, incremental rendering, and limiting the amount of content visible at once.

title: Why is repeated append() inside a large loop potentially inefficient?
answer: Repeated DOM insertion inside a large loop can cause many DOM updates and potentially trigger repeated style or layout work. A more efficient approach is to construct the required content first and insert it in fewer operations.

title: How can you optimize a jQuery table with thousands of rows?
answer: Use pagination or virtualization, minimize DOM nodes, delegate events to the table or a stable container, batch row updates, avoid repeated layout calculations, and update only the rows that changed. Server-side pagination or filtering can further reduce the amount of data rendered.

title: What is event delegation and how does it improve performance?
answer: Event delegation attaches fewer handlers to a common ancestor instead of attaching one handler to every child. For large dynamic lists, this can significantly reduce the number of event listeners and allows newly created matching elements to work automatically.

title: When should you avoid event delegation?
answer: Delegation may be inappropriate when events do not bubble as expected, when the ancestor is extremely high in the DOM and receives a very large volume of unrelated events, or when direct handlers provide substantially simpler and more predictable behavior. The event frequency and DOM structure should be considered.

title: How can you optimize mousemove and scroll events in jQuery?
answer: High-frequency events such as mousemove and scroll should not trigger expensive work on every event. Use throttling or requestAnimationFrame-based scheduling, minimize DOM reads and writes, and avoid unnecessary layout calculations.

title: What is throttling and how can it improve jQuery event performance?
answer: Throttling limits how frequently a function can execute within a given time interval. It is useful for high-frequency events such as scroll, resize, and mousemove. Instead of running expensive code hundreds of times per second, the handler can execute at a controlled frequency.

title: What is debouncing and when would you use it in jQuery?
answer: Debouncing delays execution until a specified period has passed without another event. It is useful for events such as search input, resize, and autocomplete. For example, an API request can be delayed until the user stops typing rather than sending a request for every keystroke.

title: What is the difference between throttling and debouncing?
answer: Throttling ensures that a function runs at most once within a specified interval, while debouncing waits until events stop occurring for a specified period. Throttling is commonly useful for continuous events such as scrolling, while debouncing is useful for actions such as search input.

title: How can you optimize jQuery animations?
answer: Prefer CSS transitions or animations for simple visual effects, animate transform and opacity where possible, avoid animating expensive layout properties, stop unnecessary animations, and prevent multiple animations from being queued accidentally. Browser performance tools should be used to identify rendering bottlenecks.

title: What does jQuery stop(true, true) do?
answer: stop(true, true) stops the current jQuery animation, clears queued animations, and jumps to the current animation's end state. It is useful for preventing animation queues from growing when users rapidly trigger the same interaction.

title: What is an animation queue in jQuery?
answer: jQuery effects can be queued so that multiple animations execute sequentially. If an animation is repeatedly triggered before previous animations finish, the queue can grow and cause delayed or unexpected UI behavior. Methods such as stop() can help manage unwanted queues.

title: How can you prevent jQuery animation queue buildup?
answer: Use stop(true, true) when appropriate before starting a new animation, or use CSS transitions for simple effects. You should also prevent repeated event triggers from unnecessarily starting the same animation.

title: Why should you avoid changing CSS properties repeatedly in a loop?
answer: Repeatedly changing layout-related CSS properties can cause the browser to recalculate styles and layout multiple times. A better approach is to calculate the final state first and apply it once, or toggle a CSS class that contains the required styles.

title: Why is adding a CSS class often better than repeatedly calling css()?
answer: Adding a class centralizes presentation in CSS and can reduce repeated style manipulation from JavaScript. It also improves maintainability and allows the browser to handle the visual changes through its normal style and rendering pipeline.

title: What is layout thrashing and how can it occur in jQuery?
answer: Layout thrashing occurs when code repeatedly alternates between DOM writes and layout reads, forcing the browser to recalculate layout multiple times. For example, changing an element's size and immediately reading outerHeight() repeatedly inside a loop can cause unnecessary layout work.

title: How can you prevent forced synchronous layout in jQuery?
answer: Separate DOM reads from DOM writes, cache layout measurements, batch changes, and avoid repeatedly reading properties such as dimensions immediately after modifying layout-related styles. For animation-heavy operations, requestAnimationFrame can help coordinate visual updates.

title: How can you optimize jQuery AJAX requests?
answer: Reduce unnecessary requests, debounce user-driven requests, cache responses when appropriate, request only required data, batch related operations when the API supports it, cancel obsolete requests where practical, and avoid repeatedly requesting unchanged data.

title: How can you prevent duplicate AJAX requests in jQuery?
answer: Track the active request, disable or debounce the triggering control, cache results, or cancel the previous request when only the latest request matters. For example, an autocomplete field can abort the previous request before starting a new one.

title: How do you cancel an AJAX request in jQuery?
answer: The object returned by $.ajax() provides an abort() method. For example, store the request in a variable and call request.abort() before starting a replacement request when appropriate.

title: How can AJAX response caching improve jQuery application performance?
answer: Caching prevents repeated requests for data that has not changed. jQuery can be configured for caching behavior depending on the request type and browser caching rules. Application-level caching can also store previously retrieved data and reuse it when appropriate.

title: How can you reduce network payloads in a jQuery application?
answer: Request only required fields, paginate large responses, compress HTTP responses, optimize images, remove unused JavaScript and CSS, enable appropriate caching, and use modern transport and content formats. Network payload size should be measured using browser developer tools.

title: How can you optimize JSON processing in a jQuery application?
answer: Request only the data required by the UI, avoid unnecessarily large JSON responses, minimize repeated parsing or transformations, and process large datasets incrementally where appropriate. For very large datasets, server-side filtering and pagination are often more effective than processing everything in the browser.

title: How can you improve jQuery page-load performance?
answer: Load only required JavaScript, remove unused plugins, defer non-critical scripts, optimize CSS and images, reduce DOM complexity, minimize unnecessary initialization work, cache static assets, and avoid expensive DOM operations during initial page rendering.

title: How can you reduce the impact of third-party jQuery plugins?
answer: Audit plugin necessity, remove unused plugins, load plugins only where needed, avoid duplicate dependencies, keep plugins updated, and inspect their DOM manipulation and event behavior. For frequently used functionality, replacing a large plugin with a smaller native implementation may be beneficial when practical.

title: How can you detect memory leaks in a jQuery application?
answer: Use browser developer tools to monitor heap usage, take heap snapshots, inspect detached DOM nodes, and look for objects that remain reachable unexpectedly. Common causes include forgotten event handlers, long-lived references to removed DOM elements, timers, and application-level caches.

title: How can you prevent event-handler memory leaks in jQuery?
answer: Remove handlers when components or DOM sections are destroyed using .off(), preferably with event namespaces. Avoid retaining unnecessary references to removed elements and clean up timers, subscriptions, and plugin instances during component teardown.

title: Why are event namespaces useful for jQuery cleanup?
answer: Event namespaces allow related handlers to be removed without affecting unrelated handlers. For example, $element.on('click.component', handler) can later be cleaned up with $element.off('.component'). This is particularly useful in reusable components and single-page applications.

title: How can you optimize jQuery code used in a single-page application?
answer: Use component-level initialization and cleanup, delegate events appropriately, cache DOM references, avoid duplicate handlers, clean up removed views, minimize DOM updates, lazy-load feature-specific code, and avoid keeping unnecessary references to detached DOM elements.

title: What is lazy initialization in a jQuery application?
answer: Lazy initialization means delaying setup of functionality until it is actually needed. For example, a complex date-picker plugin can be initialized only when a user opens the relevant form section. This reduces initial JavaScript execution and DOM work.

title: How can you lazy-load jQuery plugins?
answer: Load the plugin script only when the feature requiring it becomes necessary. Modern applications can use dynamic module loading or an appropriate script loader. After the plugin is loaded, initialize it for the relevant DOM elements and avoid loading the same dependency repeatedly.

title: How can you reduce jQuery bundle size?
answer: Remove unnecessary plugins and dependencies, avoid loading multiple versions of jQuery, use build tooling where appropriate, eliminate unused application code, and load feature-specific scripts only when needed. The final network payload should be measured rather than assuming that a particular optimization is beneficial.

title: How can you avoid loading jQuery on pages that do not need it?
answer: Load jQuery only on pages or application modules that require it. With a build system, dependency boundaries can be used to create separate bundles or chunks. In legacy applications, conditional script loading can also prevent unnecessary downloads.

title: How can you optimize DOM selectors in a large jQuery application?
answer: Use stable IDs or simple class selectors where appropriate, scope queries to known containers, cache frequently used collections, avoid repeatedly traversing large DOM trees, and prefer native CSS selectors supported efficiently by the browser. Profiling should be used before optimizing selectors that are not actual bottlenecks.

title: How can you improve performance when repeatedly checking element existence in jQuery?
answer: Instead of repeatedly performing the same selector, cache the result when the DOM state is stable. A jQuery collection can be checked using $element.length. If the DOM changes dynamically, the cached reference should be refreshed when necessary.

title: Why is excessive use of $(document).on() a potential performance problem?
answer: Delegating every event to the document creates a very broad event boundary. Many unrelated events may travel through that handler, increasing work and making event management harder. Delegation should generally be attached to the closest stable ancestor that can reliably handle the required events.

title: What is the performance difference between direct handlers and delegated handlers?
answer: Direct handlers can require many event listeners when applied to large collections. Delegated handlers reduce the number of listeners but require selector matching and event traversal when events occur. For large dynamic collections, delegation is often beneficial, but the best approach depends on event frequency and DOM structure.

title: How can you optimize a jQuery autocomplete search box?
answer: I would debounce input events, avoid requests for very short or unchanged queries, cancel obsolete AJAX requests, cache frequently repeated searches, limit result counts, and render only the required suggestions. Server-side filtering and pagination can further reduce response sizes.

title: How can you optimize a jQuery resize handler?
answer: Resize events can fire many times during a resize operation. Use throttling or debounce logic, avoid expensive DOM calculations on every event, cache measurements when possible, and update the UI only when the relevant breakpoint or layout state actually changes.

title: How can you optimize a jQuery scroll-based animation?
answer: Throttle or schedule scroll processing with requestAnimationFrame, avoid repeatedly querying layout properties, use CSS transforms and opacity for visual movement where appropriate, and consider Intersection Observer for visibility-based behavior instead of manually calculating positions on every scroll event.

title: Why is Intersection Observer preferable to scroll polling in some jQuery applications?
answer: Intersection Observer allows the browser to efficiently notify the application when elements enter or leave a specified intersection area. This can avoid repeatedly calculating element positions during scroll events and is useful for lazy loading, visibility tracking, and infinite-scroll implementations.

title: How would you diagnose a slow jQuery page in a production environment?
answer: I would first reproduce and measure the issue using browser performance tools. I would inspect JavaScript execution, long tasks, DOM size, layout and paint activity, network requests, memory usage, event-handler frequency, and AJAX latency. Then I would identify the largest bottleneck, apply a targeted optimization, and measure the result again rather than making speculative changes.
