title: What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript?
answer: var is function-scoped and can be redeclared. let and const are block-scoped and cannot be redeclared in the same scope. A const variable cannot be reassigned after initialization, although objects and arrays declared with const can still have their contents modified.

title: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
answer: Hoisting describes how JavaScript processes declarations before executing code. Function declarations are available before their position in the source. var declarations are initialized with undefined, while let and const declarations remain uninitialized in the Temporal Dead Zone until execution reaches their declaration.

title: What is the Temporal Dead Zone?
answer: The Temporal Dead Zone, or TDZ, is the period between entering a scope and reaching the declaration of a let, const, or class declaration. Accessing the variable during this period throws a ReferenceError.

title: What is lexical scope in JavaScript?
answer: Lexical scope means that the availability of variables is determined by where variables and functions are written in the source code. Inner functions can access variables from their outer lexical environments, which is the foundation for closures.

title: What is a closure in JavaScript?
answer: A closure is created when a function retains access to variables from its surrounding lexical environment even after the outer function has finished executing. Closures are commonly used for data privacy, callbacks, function factories, and maintaining state.

title: What are practical use cases of closures?
answer: Closures are useful for creating private state, function factories, memoization, callbacks, event handlers, and maintaining state between function calls. For example, a counter function can keep its count variable private through a closure.

title: What is the difference between lexical scope and dynamic scope?
answer: JavaScript uses lexical scope, meaning variable resolution depends on where code is written. Dynamic scope would determine variable resolution based on the runtime call stack. JavaScript does not use dynamic scoping for normal variable lookup.

title: What is the difference between function scope and block scope?
answer: Function scope means a variable is accessible throughout the function in which it is declared, as with var. Block scope limits a variable to the surrounding block, such as an if, for, or { } block. let and const are block-scoped.

title: What is the difference between == and ===?
answer: == performs loose equality comparison and may perform type coercion before comparing values. === performs strict equality comparison and requires both operands to have compatible types and equal values. In most application code, === is preferred because its behavior is more predictable.

title: What is type coercion in JavaScript?
answer: Type coercion is the conversion of a value from one type to another. JavaScript performs implicit coercion in many operations, such as converting strings and numbers during certain comparisons or arithmetic expressions. Developers can also explicitly convert values using functions such as Number(), String(), and Boolean().

title: What is the difference between null and undefined?
answer: undefined commonly represents an absent or uninitialized value, such as a declared variable without an assigned value or a missing object property. null is an explicit value that represents the intentional absence of an object value. They are distinct values and types, although loose equality considers them equal.

title: What is the difference between primitive and reference values?
answer: Primitive values include strings, numbers, booleans, BigInt, symbols, undefined, and null. Objects, arrays, and functions are objects and are handled through references. Assigning a primitive copies its value, while assigning an object copies the reference to the same underlying object.

title: What are the primitive data types in JavaScript?
answer: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, and null. Everything else is an object, including arrays and functions.

title: What is the difference between Number and BigInt?
answer: Number uses IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point representation and safely represents integers only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. BigInt supports integers of arbitrary size. BigInt values cannot be mixed directly with Number values in arithmetic operations without explicit conversion.

title: What is NaN in JavaScript?
answer: NaN means Not-a-Number and represents an invalid numeric result. Interestingly, NaN is not equal to itself using ===. The recommended way to test for the special NaN value is Number.isNaN().

title: What is the difference between Number.isNaN() and global isNaN()?
answer: Number.isNaN() checks whether the value is actually the numeric NaN value without performing type coercion. The global isNaN() converts its argument to a number before checking, which can produce surprising results. Number.isNaN() is generally safer for strict checks.

title: What are truthy and falsy values?
answer: Truthy values behave like true when converted to boolean, while falsy values behave like false. Common falsy values include false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, and NaN. Objects and arrays are truthy, even when empty.

title: What is the difference between || and ?? operators?
answer: The logical OR operator || uses the right-hand value when the left-hand value is falsy. The nullish coalescing operator ?? uses the right-hand value only when the left-hand value is null or undefined. Therefore, 0 and an empty string are preserved by ??.

title: What is optional chaining in JavaScript?
answer: Optional chaining, written using ?., safely accesses properties, methods, or indexed values when an intermediate value may be null or undefined. Instead of throwing an error, the expression evaluates to undefined when the optional chain cannot continue.

title: What is the nullish coalescing assignment operator?
answer: The ??= operator assigns a value only when the left-hand side is null or undefined. For example, user.name ??= 'Guest' assigns Guest only when user.name is nullish.

title: What is destructuring in JavaScript?
answer: Destructuring allows values to be extracted from arrays or properties to be extracted from objects into variables. For example, const { name, age } = user extracts properties from an object. It can make code more concise when working with structured data.

title: What is the difference between object and array destructuring?
answer: Object destructuring extracts values based on property names, while array destructuring extracts values based on position. For example, const { name } = user uses an object property, while const [first, second] = items uses array indexes.

title: What are default parameters in JavaScript?
answer: Default parameters provide fallback values for function parameters when the corresponding argument is undefined. For example, function greet(name = 'Guest') {} uses Guest when no value or an explicit undefined is supplied.

title: What are rest and spread operators?
answer: Both use the ... syntax but serve different purposes. The rest syntax collects remaining values into an array or object, while the spread syntax expands iterable or object values into another expression. For example, function sum(...nums) uses rest, while [...arr1, ...arr2] uses spread.

title: What is the difference between spread and Object.assign()?
answer: Both can create shallow copies or merge object properties. Object spread, such as { ...user }, provides concise syntax, while Object.assign() copies properties into a target object. Both perform shallow copying and do not recursively clone nested objects.

title: What is a shallow copy in JavaScript?
answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer object or array while preserving references to nested objects. For example, { ...user } creates a new user object, but a nested address object remains shared between the original and the copy.

title: What is a deep copy in JavaScript?
answer: A deep copy creates independent copies of nested structures rather than preserving references to the original nested objects. Modern JavaScript provides structuredClone() for many data types. JSON serialization can also clone some data structures but has important limitations and should not be treated as a general-purpose deep-copy mechanism.

title: What is structuredClone()?
answer: structuredClone() creates a deep copy of many JavaScript values using the structured clone algorithm. It supports more data types than JSON serialization and can preserve certain built-in structures. It does not clone every possible JavaScript value, such as functions.

title: What is the difference between Object.freeze(), Object.seal(), and Object.preventExtensions()?
answer: Object.preventExtensions() prevents new properties from being added. Object.seal() additionally prevents properties from being deleted or reconfigured. Object.freeze() additionally prevents changing existing data properties. These operations are shallow and do not recursively freeze nested objects.

title: What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
answer: for...in iterates over enumerable property keys, including inherited enumerable properties unless filtered. for...of iterates over values produced by an iterable, such as an array, string, Map, or Set. For arrays, for...of is generally appropriate when you need the values.

title: What is an iterable in JavaScript?
answer: An iterable is an object that implements the iterable protocol by providing a Symbol.iterator method. Iterables can be consumed by constructs such as for...of, the spread operator, and array destructuring. Arrays, strings, Maps, and Sets are common iterables.

title: What is an iterator in JavaScript?
answer: An iterator is an object that follows the iterator protocol by providing a next() method. Each call to next() returns an object containing value and done. Iterators are used to implement JavaScript's iterable behavior.

title: What are generators in JavaScript?
answer: Generators are functions declared with function* that can pause and resume execution using the yield keyword. Calling a generator function returns an iterator. Generators are useful for creating custom iterators and controlling incremental execution.

title: What is the difference between yield and return in a generator?
answer: yield pauses generator execution and produces a value while allowing execution to continue later. return finishes the generator and marks the iterator as done. A generator can yield multiple values but normally completes after its return or natural termination.

title: What is a callback function?
answer: A callback is a function passed to another function so that it can be invoked later. Callbacks are commonly used for event handlers, array methods, asynchronous operations, and custom control flow.

title: What is callback hell and how can it be avoided?
answer: Callback hell refers to deeply nested callbacks that make asynchronous code difficult to read, maintain, and handle errors in. It can be reduced by using named functions, modularizing logic, Promises, async/await, and appropriate abstraction of asynchronous operations.

title: What is a Promise in JavaScript?
answer: A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation. It has three conceptual states: pending, fulfilled, and rejected. Promises can be consumed using then(), catch(), and finally().

title: What is the difference between Promise.all(), Promise.allSettled(), Promise.race(), and Promise.any()?
answer: Promise.all() fulfills when all promises fulfill and rejects when one rejects. Promise.allSettled() waits for every promise and reports each result. Promise.race() settles when the first promise settles. Promise.any() fulfills when the first promise fulfills and rejects only when all input promises reject.

title: What is async/await?
answer: async/await provides syntax for working with Promises in a more synchronous-looking style. An async function always returns a Promise, while await pauses execution within that async function until the awaited Promise settles.

title: What happens when an async function throws an error?
answer: If an async function throws an error, the Promise returned by that function becomes rejected with the thrown error. The rejection can be handled using try...catch around an await expression or by using .catch() on the returned Promise.

title: What is the JavaScript event loop?
answer: The event loop coordinates execution of JavaScript code with asynchronous tasks. JavaScript executes synchronous code on the call stack, while asynchronous operations are handled by the host environment. When the stack becomes available, queued jobs and tasks are processed according to the event-loop rules.

title: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?
answer: Microtasks include Promise reaction jobs and are processed after the current JavaScript execution completes before the event loop proceeds to the next task in typical browser execution. Tasks, sometimes called macrotasks, include operations such as timers and certain I/O or user-interaction events. Understanding their ordering is important when reasoning about asynchronous code.

title: What is the call stack in JavaScript?
answer: The call stack tracks active JavaScript function calls. When a function is called, a stack frame is added; when it returns, the frame is removed. Deep or infinite recursion can exhaust the call stack and result in a stack overflow.

title: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript?
answer: Synchronous code executes sequentially and normally blocks further JavaScript execution until the current operation completes. Asynchronous programming allows work to be initiated without waiting for its completion before continuing other work. Promises, async/await, timers, and browser APIs are commonly used for asynchronous operations.

title: What is setTimeout() and is it guaranteed to execute after exactly the specified delay?
answer: setTimeout() schedules a callback to be placed into the task queue after at least the specified delay. It does not guarantee exact execution time because the callback must wait for the call stack and event-loop scheduling. Long-running JavaScript can therefore delay its execution.

title: What is the difference between setTimeout(fn, 0) and immediately calling fn()?
answer: Calling fn() executes the function synchronously during the current call stack. setTimeout(fn, 0) schedules the callback as a future task, so it runs only after the current synchronous execution completes and the event loop reaches that task.

title: What is this in JavaScript?
answer: this refers to a value determined by how a function is called, except for arrow functions, which capture this lexically from their surrounding scope. In a method call, it generally refers to the receiver object; with constructors it refers to the newly created instance; with explicit binding, methods such as call(), apply(), and bind() can control it.

title: What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?
answer: call() invokes a function immediately with a specified this value and individual arguments. apply() also invokes it immediately but accepts arguments as an array-like value. bind() returns a new function with the specified this value and optionally preconfigured arguments.

title: How is this different inside an arrow function?
answer: Arrow functions do not create their own this binding. They capture this from the surrounding lexical scope. Therefore, calling an arrow function with call(), apply(), or bind() does not change its lexical this.

title: What is a higher-order function?
answer: A higher-order function is a function that takes one or more functions as arguments, returns a function, or both. Examples include map(), filter(), and reduce(). Higher-order functions are a fundamental part of functional programming in JavaScript.

title: What is a pure function in JavaScript?
answer: A pure function always produces the same output for the same input and does not cause observable side effects outside the function. Pure functions are easier to test, reason about, and reuse.

title: What is an impure function?
answer: An impure function either depends on external state or produces side effects. Examples include modifying a global variable, changing an external object, performing DOM manipulation, or making an API request.

title: What is function composition in JavaScript?
answer: Function composition combines multiple functions so that the output of one function becomes the input of another. It allows complex behavior to be built from smaller reusable functions.

title: What is currying in JavaScript?
answer: Currying transforms a function that accepts multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each accept one or more arguments. For example, add(2)(3) can represent a curried version of an addition function.

title: What is partial application?
answer: Partial application creates a new function by pre-filling some arguments of an existing function. Unlike currying, partial application does not necessarily require one argument per function invocation.

title: What is memoization in JavaScript?
answer: Memoization is an optimization technique where the result of a function is cached based on its inputs. When the same inputs are provided again, the cached result can be returned instead of recalculating it.

title: How would you implement memoization in JavaScript?
answer: A common implementation uses a Map or object as a cache. The function arguments are converted into a suitable cache key, and the computed result is stored. On subsequent calls with the same inputs, the cached result is returned.

title: What is recursion in JavaScript?
answer: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. A recursive function must have a base condition to prevent infinite recursion and eventual stack overflow.

title: What is tail recursion?
answer: Tail recursion occurs when the recursive function call is the final operation performed by the function. Some programming languages optimize tail calls, but developers should not assume general JavaScript environments will eliminate recursive stack frames for ordinary tail-recursive code.

title: What is the difference between map(), filter(), and reduce()?
answer: map() transforms every element and returns a new array. filter() returns elements that satisfy a condition. reduce() combines array elements into a single accumulated result, such as a number, object, or another array.

title: What is the difference between forEach() and map()?
answer: forEach() is generally used for side effects and returns undefined. map() transforms each element and returns a new array containing the results. Use map() when you need the transformed array.

title: Can you break or return from forEach()?
answer: You cannot use break to exit a forEach() loop. A return only returns from the callback, not from the surrounding function. If early termination is required, a for...of loop or methods such as some() or find() may be more appropriate.

title: What is the difference between some(), every(), find(), and findIndex()?
answer: some() returns true if at least one element satisfies a condition. every() returns true if all elements satisfy it. find() returns the first matching element, while findIndex() returns the index of the first matching element.

title: What is the difference between find() and filter()?
answer: find() returns the first matching element and stops searching once it finds one. filter() evaluates the condition across the array and returns a new array containing all matching elements.

title: What is the difference between slice() and splice()?
answer: slice() creates a shallow copy of a portion of an array without modifying the original array. splice() modifies the original array by adding, removing, or replacing elements.

title: What is the difference between concat() and spread syntax?
answer: Both can combine arrays. concat() returns a new array and can concatenate values or arrays, while spread syntax such as [...a, ...b] expands iterable values into a new array. Spread is often more concise for combining arrays.

title: What is Array.from()?
answer: Array.from() creates a new array from an iterable or array-like object. It can also accept a mapping function, making it useful for converting structures such as NodeLists or strings into arrays.

title: What is the difference between Array.from() and the spread operator?
answer: Both can convert iterables into arrays. Array.from() can additionally accept a mapping function and can work with certain array-like objects that are not necessarily iterable. Spread requires an iterable for this use case.

title: What is Array.of()?
answer: Array.of() creates a new array from its arguments. It differs from the Array constructor because Array.of(5) creates [5], while new Array(5) creates an array with length 5 and no elements.

title: What is the difference between flat() and flatMap()?
answer: flat() flattens nested arrays by a specified depth. flatMap() first maps each element and then flattens the result by one level. flatMap() is useful when each input element can produce zero or multiple output elements.

title: What is Array.prototype.reduce() commonly used for?
answer: reduce() can calculate totals, group records, create lookup objects, flatten structures, build maps, and perform many other accumulations. It takes an accumulator and current value and returns the updated accumulator for the next iteration.

title: What is a Set in JavaScript?
answer: Set is a collection that stores unique values. It is useful for removing duplicates, checking membership, and maintaining a collection where duplicate values should not exist.

title: What is a Map in JavaScript?
answer: Map is a key-value collection where keys can be values of any JavaScript type. It provides methods such as set(), get(), has(), and delete(), and it preserves insertion order during iteration.

title: What is the difference between Object and Map?
answer: Objects are primarily used for structured records and have a prototype-based model. Maps are dedicated key-value collections and support keys of any type, explicit size tracking, and convenient iteration. Maps can be preferable when dynamically managing arbitrary key-value entries.

title: What is WeakMap in JavaScript?
answer: WeakMap stores key-value pairs where keys must be objects or non-registered symbols. Its keys are weakly held, meaning they can be garbage-collected when there are no other strong references to them. WeakMaps are useful for associating private metadata with objects.

title: What is WeakSet in JavaScript?
answer: WeakSet stores objects or non-registered symbols weakly. It is useful when you need to track object membership without preventing those objects from being garbage-collected.

title: Why can't you iterate directly over a WeakMap?
answer: WeakMap is intentionally not enumerable. Because its keys may disappear through garbage collection at any time, exposing a stable enumeration of all entries would conflict with its weak-reference semantics.

title: What is Symbol in JavaScript?
answer: Symbol creates unique primitive values. Symbols are commonly used as unique object property keys and for well-known protocols such as Symbol.iterator. Two separately created symbols are unique even if they have the same description.

title: What is the difference between Symbol() and Symbol.for()?
answer: Symbol() creates a new unique symbol every time it is called. Symbol.for() uses the global symbol registry, so repeated calls with the same key return the same symbol.

title: What are well-known symbols?
answer: Well-known symbols are predefined symbols that customize JavaScript language behavior. Examples include Symbol.iterator, Symbol.toPrimitive, Symbol.toStringTag, and Symbol.asyncIterator.

title: What is the prototype chain?
answer: The prototype chain is the mechanism JavaScript uses to resolve inherited properties and methods. When a property is not found directly on an object, JavaScript looks at its prototype and continues through the prototype chain until the property is found or the chain ends.

title: What is the difference between __proto__ and prototype?
answer: prototype is a property commonly found on constructor functions and is used as the prototype for objects created with new. __proto__ is an accessor that exposes an object's prototype. Modern code should generally use Object.getPrototypeOf() and Object.setPrototypeOf() rather than directly relying on __proto__.

title: What does Object.create() do?
answer: Object.create() creates a new object with a specified prototype. For example, Object.create(parent) creates an object whose prototype is parent. It can be used to create objects with controlled prototype relationships.

title: What is prototypal inheritance?
answer: Prototypal inheritance allows an object to access properties and methods from another object through its prototype chain. JavaScript's class syntax provides a more familiar syntax for creating prototype-based inheritance relationships but does not replace the underlying prototype mechanism.

title: What is a JavaScript class?
answer: A class is syntax for defining constructor behavior and methods for objects. JavaScript classes are built on top of the language's prototype-based inheritance model. Classes can define constructors, instance methods, static methods, fields, private fields, and inheritance.

title: What is the constructor method in a JavaScript class?
answer: The constructor() method is used to initialize a newly created class instance. It is automatically called when the class is instantiated using new. A class can have only one constructor definition.

title: What are static methods in JavaScript classes?
answer: Static methods belong to the class itself rather than individual instances. They are called using the class name, such as User.create(), rather than through an instance like user.create().

title: What are private class fields?
answer: Private class fields use the # prefix and are accessible only within the class that declares them. For example, #balance cannot be accessed directly from outside the class. They provide language-level encapsulation for class state.

title: What is the difference between extends and composition?
answer: extends establishes an inheritance relationship between classes. Composition builds objects by combining smaller behaviors or objects rather than inheriting from a parent class. Composition often provides more flexibility because behavior can be combined without creating deep inheritance hierarchies.

title: What is a getter and setter in JavaScript?
answer: A getter defines a method that is accessed like a property, while a setter defines behavior when a property is assigned. They can be declared using get and set in object literals or classes and are useful for validation, computed values, and controlled access to internal state.

title: What is Object.defineProperty()?
answer: Object.defineProperty() defines or modifies a property with descriptors such as value, writable, enumerable, and configurable. It provides precise control over an object's property behavior.

title: What are property descriptors in JavaScript?
answer: Property descriptors define how an object property behaves. Data descriptors use value and writable, while accessor descriptors use get and set. Both types can also have enumerable and configurable attributes.

title: What is the difference between enumerable and non-enumerable properties?
answer: Enumerable properties are included in operations such as Object.keys() and for...in under their respective rules. Non-enumerable properties are not included by those enumeration mechanisms. Property descriptors can be used to control enumerability.

title: What is Object.keys(), Object.values(), and Object.entries()?
answer: Object.keys() returns an array of an object's own enumerable property names. Object.values() returns the corresponding values. Object.entries() returns key-value pairs as nested arrays. These methods are useful for iterating over object data.

title: What is the difference between Object.keys() and for...in?
answer: Object.keys() returns an array containing an object's own enumerable property keys. for...in iterates over enumerable string properties, including inherited enumerable properties. When using for...in, inheritance should be considered or filtered appropriately.

title: What is Object.hasOwn()?
answer: Object.hasOwn() checks whether an object has a specified property as its own property rather than inheriting it from the prototype chain. It is a convenient modern alternative to patterns such as Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key).

title: What is the difference between hasOwnProperty() and the in operator?
answer: hasOwnProperty() checks only whether a property belongs directly to the object. The in operator checks both the object and its prototype chain. Therefore, key in obj can return true for inherited properties.

title: What is JSON.stringify()?
answer: JSON.stringify() converts a JavaScript value into a JSON string when the value is representable in JSON. It is commonly used for sending structured data over HTTP or storing JSON-compatible data. It does not preserve every JavaScript type or object behavior.

title: What is JSON.parse()?
answer: JSON.parse() converts a valid JSON string into the corresponding JavaScript value. Invalid JSON causes a SyntaxError, so untrusted or external JSON should be parsed with appropriate error handling.

title: What values are not preserved by JSON.stringify()?
answer: JSON cannot represent values such as functions, symbols, and undefined in the general object representation. Special numeric values such as NaN and Infinity are serialized as null. Dates are serialized through their JSON representation, and circular references cause serialization to fail.

title: What is a JavaScript execution context?
answer: An execution context is the environment in which JavaScript code is evaluated and executed. It contains information such as variable bindings, the scope chain, and the value of this. Common contexts include the global execution context, function execution contexts, and module execution contexts.

title: What is the global execution context?
answer: The global execution context is created when a JavaScript program starts. It initializes global bindings and provides the environment in which top-level code executes. In browsers, the global object is commonly represented by window, while globalThis provides a standard cross-environment reference.

title: What is the execution context creation phase?
answer: Before executing code, JavaScript establishes the execution environment, including lexical and variable bindings and other execution-context information. Function declarations and variable bindings are processed according to their declaration semantics before the corresponding statements execute.

title: What is the execution phase in JavaScript?
answer: During the execution phase, JavaScript evaluates statements and expressions using the bindings established for the current execution context. Function calls create new execution contexts, and those contexts are added to the call stack while they execute.

title: What is the scope chain?
answer: The scope chain is the sequence of lexical environments JavaScript searches when resolving an identifier. If a variable is not found in the current scope, JavaScript looks through enclosing lexical environments until it finds the binding or reaches the end of the chain.

title: What is the difference between lexical environment and execution context?
answer: A lexical environment is a specification concept representing bindings and their relationship to an outer environment. An execution context describes the broader runtime state used while executing code. An execution context references the relevant lexical environments for variable resolution.

title: What happens when a function is invoked in JavaScript?
answer: A new function execution context is created and placed on the call stack. Parameters and local bindings are initialized, the function body executes, and the context is removed from the stack when the function completes or throws an exception.

title: What is the difference between declaration and expression in JavaScript?
answer: A declaration introduces a binding or other program construct, such as a function declaration or variable declaration. An expression produces a value and can appear where a value is expected. For example, function add() {} is a function declaration, while const add = function() {} contains a function expression.

title: What is a function expression?
answer: A function expression creates a function as part of an expression. It can be assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, or returned from another function. Function expressions can be anonymous or named.

title: What is a named function expression?
answer: A named function expression assigns a name to the function itself, such as const factorial = function fact(n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1); }. The internal name can be useful for recursion and debugging.

title: What is an immediately invoked function expression?
answer: An IIFE is a function expression that is executed immediately after it is created. A common pattern is (function() { ... })();. Historically, IIFEs were widely used to create private scopes before block-scoped declarations and JavaScript modules became common.

title: What are first-class functions in JavaScript?
answer: Functions are first-class values in JavaScript, meaning they can be assigned to variables, stored in data structures, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. This capability enables callbacks, higher-order functions, closures, and functional programming patterns.

title: What is a function factory?
answer: A function factory is a function that creates and returns another function. The returned function can capture configuration or state from the factory through a closure. This is useful for creating specialized reusable functions.

title: What is an arrow function?
answer: An arrow function provides concise function syntax and uses lexical this instead of creating its own this binding. Arrow functions are commonly used for callbacks and functional operations such as map(), filter(), and reduce().

title: Can arrow functions be used as constructors?
answer: No. Arrow functions do not have the internal constructor behavior required by new. Attempting to use an arrow function with new results in a TypeError.

title: Why do arrow functions not have their own arguments object?
answer: Arrow functions do not create their own arguments binding. If arguments are needed, use rest parameters such as (...args), which provide an actual array containing the arguments.

title: What is the arguments object?
answer: The arguments object is an array-like object available inside traditional non-arrow functions. It contains the arguments passed to the function. Modern code often prefers rest parameters because they provide a real array and clearer semantics.

title: What is the difference between arguments and rest parameters?
answer: arguments is an array-like object available in traditional functions, while rest parameters collect remaining arguments into a real array. Rest parameters are generally more explicit and work naturally with array methods.

title: What happens when a function does not explicitly return a value?
answer: The function returns undefined. This is true for functions that reach the end without a return statement and for functions that execute return; without a value.

title: What is an exception in JavaScript?
answer: An exception is an abnormal condition that interrupts normal execution and transfers control to exception-handling logic. JavaScript can throw values using throw, although throwing Error objects is generally preferred for useful debugging information.

title: How does try...catch...finally work?
answer: try contains code that may throw an exception. catch handles an exception if one occurs, while finally executes after the try/catch processing regardless of whether an exception occurred. The finally block is commonly used for cleanup.

title: What is the difference between throw and return?
answer: return completes the current function and provides a value to its caller. throw interrupts normal execution and propagates an exception until a matching handler is found. They represent different control-flow mechanisms.

title: What are custom errors in JavaScript?
answer: Custom errors can be created by extending the built-in Error class. For example, class ValidationError extends Error {} creates a specialized error type that can be identified separately when handling exceptions.

title: What is the difference between Error, TypeError, ReferenceError, and SyntaxError?
answer: Error is the general base error type. TypeError commonly indicates an operation was performed on an inappropriate value type. ReferenceError occurs when an identifier cannot be resolved appropriately. SyntaxError indicates invalid JavaScript syntax.

title: What is strict mode in JavaScript?
answer: Strict mode enables stricter JavaScript semantics and prevents or changes certain error-prone behaviors. It can be enabled using 'use strict';. JavaScript modules and class bodies are automatically strict mode code.

title: What are the benefits of strict mode?
answer: Strict mode catches certain programming mistakes earlier, prevents accidental creation of global variables, changes some this behavior in ordinary functions, and disallows several legacy features. It helps make code more predictable and easier to maintain.

title: What is an ES module?
answer: An ES module is a JavaScript file that uses the standard import and export syntax to define module dependencies and public APIs. Modules have their own scope and are automatically executed in strict mode.

title: What is the difference between named export and default export?
answer: A named export has an explicit exported name and can have multiple exports from a module. A default export provides one primary exported value for the module. Named exports are imported using matching names, while default exports can be imported with a locally chosen name.

title: What is dynamic import()?
answer: import() dynamically loads a module and returns a Promise that resolves to the module namespace object. It is useful for lazy loading, code splitting, and loading functionality only when it is needed.

title: What is tree shaking?
answer: Tree shaking is a build-time optimization that removes unused exports from JavaScript modules when the tooling can safely determine they are not needed. It works particularly well with statically analyzable ES module imports and exports.

title: What is code splitting?
answer: Code splitting divides an application's JavaScript into multiple chunks that can be loaded independently. This can reduce the initial JavaScript payload and allow features to be loaded on demand, commonly through dynamic imports and bundler configuration.

title: What is a JavaScript module namespace object?
answer: A module namespace object represents the exported bindings of an ES module. It is returned by dynamic import() and can be accessed using the exported names, such as module.default or module.someFunction.

title: What is top-level await?
answer: Top-level await allows an ES module to use await directly at module scope without wrapping it inside an async function. It can delay module evaluation until the awaited operation completes, so it should be used thoughtfully.

title: What is the difference between script and module scripts?
answer: Classic scripts execute using traditional script semantics and share the relevant global environment. Module scripts have their own module scope, support import and export, are automatically strict, and are deferred by default when loaded through HTML's module mechanism.

title: What is event delegation using native JavaScript?
answer: Native event delegation attaches an event listener to a stable ancestor and checks the event target or uses methods such as closest() to determine which descendant triggered the event. It reduces the number of listeners and works well for dynamically created elements.

title: What is the difference between event.target.closest() and matches()?
answer: matches() checks whether an element itself matches a selector. closest() checks the element itself and then walks up its ancestors until it finds a matching element. Both are useful for implementing event delegation.

title: What is CustomEvent in JavaScript?
answer: CustomEvent allows applications to create custom DOM events. Additional information can be supplied through the detail property. The event can then be dispatched using dispatchEvent() and handled with addEventListener().

title: What is dispatchEvent()?
answer: dispatchEvent() synchronously dispatches a DOM event on a target object. Event listeners registered for that event can respond according to the event's propagation and cancellation rules.

title: What is preventDefault() in native DOM events?
answer: preventDefault() tells the browser not to perform the default action associated with a cancelable event. For example, it can prevent a form submission or link navigation when application logic needs to handle the action itself.

title: What is AbortController?
answer: AbortController provides a standard mechanism for signaling cancellation to APIs that support an AbortSignal. It is commonly used to cancel fetch() requests when they are no longer needed, such as when a user changes a search query.

title: How do you cancel a fetch request?
answer: Create an AbortController, pass its signal to fetch(), and call controller.abort() when cancellation is required. The fetch Promise rejects with an abort-related error, which should be handled appropriately.

title: What is the Fetch API?
answer: The Fetch API provides a Promise-based interface for making HTTP requests. It uses fetch() to request resources and returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object. Unlike some older AJAX APIs, HTTP error status codes do not automatically reject the fetch Promise.

title: How do you handle HTTP errors with fetch()?
answer: Fetch resolves its Promise for HTTP responses such as 404 or 500. Therefore, code should explicitly check response.ok or response.status and throw or handle an application error when the response is not successful.

title: What is the difference between fetch() and XMLHttpRequest?
answer: Fetch provides a modern Promise-based API with a cleaner interface for HTTP requests. XMLHttpRequest is an older event-based API with broader legacy usage. Fetch integrates naturally with async/await and supports modern features such as AbortController.

title: What is localStorage?
answer: localStorage provides persistent client-side key-value storage associated with an origin. Values are stored as strings and normally remain available across browser sessions until they are removed or the relevant storage is cleared.

title: What is sessionStorage?
answer: sessionStorage provides string-based key-value storage associated with an origin and a browser tab or window session. Its lifetime is generally tied to that page session rather than being persistent in the same way as localStorage.

title: What are the limitations of localStorage?
answer: localStorage stores only strings, has limited storage capacity compared with server-side databases, is synchronous, and is accessible to JavaScript running in the page's origin. It should not be used to store sensitive credentials such as long-lived authentication secrets when a safer architecture is available.

title: What is the StorageEvent?
answer: The storage event is fired in other documents of the same origin when a localStorage value changes. It can be used for simple cross-tab synchronization. The event is not fired in the same document that made the storage change.

title: What is IndexedDB?
answer: IndexedDB is a browser database API for storing larger amounts of structured data locally. It supports object stores, indexes, transactions, and asynchronous operations. It is more suitable than localStorage for complex or larger client-side datasets.

title: What is the Cache API?
answer: The Cache API provides programmatic storage of request and response pairs. It is commonly used with service workers to implement caching strategies for web applications and Progressive Web Apps. Unlike localStorage, it is designed around HTTP request and response objects.

title: What is a service worker in JavaScript?
answer: A service worker is a background script that runs separately from the web page and can intercept network requests, manage caching, support offline experiences, and handle certain background events. It operates under security restrictions and requires HTTPS in production environments.

title: What is a Web Worker?
answer: A Web Worker allows JavaScript to execute in a background thread separate from the main UI thread. It is useful for CPU-intensive tasks that could otherwise block rendering and user interaction. Workers communicate with the main thread using message passing.

title: What is the difference between Web Worker and Service Worker?
answer: A Web Worker is primarily used for running JavaScript off the main thread. A Service Worker is a specialized worker designed to act as a programmable network proxy for its controlled pages and support capabilities such as caching and offline functionality. Service Workers also have lifecycle and scope rules that differ from ordinary workers.

title: What is SharedWorker?
answer: A SharedWorker can be shared by multiple browsing contexts, such as tabs or windows, that belong to the same origin and satisfy its scope rules. Communication occurs through ports. It can be useful when multiple pages need to communicate with a shared background execution context.

title: How do Web Workers communicate with the main thread?
answer: Workers communicate using message passing. The main thread can call worker.postMessage(), and the worker can respond using postMessage(). Message handlers such as onmessage receive the transferred or cloned data.

title: What is the structured clone algorithm?
answer: The structured clone algorithm is used by browser APIs to copy many JavaScript values between execution contexts. It supports various built-in data structures and avoids sharing ordinary object references between contexts. Some values, such as functions, cannot be structured-cloned.

title: What are transferable objects in JavaScript?
answer: Transferable objects can have their underlying resources transferred from one execution context to another instead of being copied. Examples include certain ArrayBuffer-based resources and MessagePort. After transfer, the original context generally loses access to the transferred resource.

title: What is SharedArrayBuffer?
answer: SharedArrayBuffer provides memory that can be shared between certain JavaScript execution contexts such as workers. It enables shared-memory communication and can be combined with Atomics. Browsers impose security requirements for enabling shared memory.

title: What is Atomics in JavaScript?
answer: The Atomics API provides atomic operations on shared typed-array memory. It helps coordinate concurrent access to shared memory and can provide synchronization mechanisms such as waiting and notification.

title: What is requestAnimationFrame()?
answer: requestAnimationFrame() schedules a callback to run before the browser performs the next repaint. It is commonly used for smooth visual updates and animations because it allows JavaScript animation work to synchronize with the browser's rendering cycle.

title: What is the difference between requestAnimationFrame() and setInterval() for animations?
answer: requestAnimationFrame() is designed for visual updates and synchronizes with the browser's rendering cycle. setInterval() runs callbacks according to a timer and is not synchronized with rendering. For browser animations, requestAnimationFrame is generally the better choice.

title: What is cancelAnimationFrame()?
answer: cancelAnimationFrame() cancels a previously scheduled animation-frame callback. The identifier returned by requestAnimationFrame() is passed to cancelAnimationFrame().

title: What is requestIdleCallback()?
answer: requestIdleCallback() allows code to be scheduled during periods when the browser is idle. It can be useful for low-priority background work, although developers should account for browser support and should not use it for time-critical operations.

title: What is the Page Visibility API?
answer: The Page Visibility API allows code to determine whether a document is currently visible to the user. The visibilitychange event can be used to pause unnecessary work, animations, polling, or media activity when a page becomes hidden.

title: How can you optimize JavaScript when a browser tab becomes inactive?
answer: Listen for the visibilitychange event and pause unnecessary polling, animations, timers, or expensive calculations when the document becomes hidden. Resume the required work when visibility is restored. This can reduce CPU and battery consumption.

title: What is the MutationObserver API?
answer: MutationObserver asynchronously observes changes to the DOM, such as added or removed nodes, attribute changes, and text changes. It is useful when code needs to react to dynamic DOM modifications without repeatedly polling the DOM.

title: What is the ResizeObserver API?
answer: ResizeObserver observes changes to the size of an element's content or border box. It is useful for responsive components that need to react to their own size rather than relying only on viewport resize events.

title: What is the IntersectionObserver API?
answer: IntersectionObserver asynchronously observes whether an element intersects a specified viewport or ancestor. It is commonly used for lazy loading, infinite scrolling, visibility tracking, and triggering animations when elements enter the viewport.

title: What is the BroadcastChannel API?
answer: BroadcastChannel allows same-origin browsing contexts to communicate by sending messages through a named channel. It can be used for cross-tab synchronization, such as notifying other tabs that application state has changed.

title: What is postMessage()?
answer: postMessage() enables controlled communication between different browsing contexts or execution contexts, such as windows, iframes, and workers. The receiving side should validate the message's origin and content before processing it.

title: What security consideration is important when using window.postMessage()?
answer: The receiver should validate event.origin and should not blindly trust message data. Using a wildcard target origin when sending sensitive information should be avoided. Message handlers should also validate the structure and meaning of received data.

title: What is the same-origin policy?
answer: The same-origin policy is a browser security mechanism that restricts how documents and scripts from one origin can interact with resources from another origin. An origin is determined by scheme, host, and port. Cross-origin access is selectively enabled through mechanisms such as CORS.

title: What is CORS?
answer: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, or CORS, is a browser mechanism that allows servers to specify which cross-origin requests are permitted. Servers communicate these permissions through HTTP response headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

title: What is a preflight request in CORS?
answer: A CORS preflight is an HTTP OPTIONS request sent by the browser before certain cross-origin requests. It allows the browser to determine whether the server permits the intended method, headers, and origin before sending the actual request.

title: What is XSS and how can JavaScript applications prevent it?
answer: Cross-Site Scripting, or XSS, occurs when attacker-controlled content is interpreted as executable code in a user's browser. Prevention includes safely handling untrusted data, avoiding unsafe HTML insertion, using appropriate output encoding, sanitizing HTML when HTML is required, and implementing security controls such as Content Security Policy.

title: What is the difference between innerHTML and textContent?
answer: innerHTML interprets assigned strings as HTML markup, while textContent treats the value as plain text. When displaying untrusted user input, textContent is generally safer because it does not parse the value as HTML.

title: What is DOM-based XSS?
answer: DOM-based XSS occurs when client-side JavaScript takes attacker-controlled data from a source such as the URL and uses it in an unsafe DOM operation. Examples include assigning untrusted data to innerHTML or dangerous URL-related APIs without proper validation or sanitization.

title: What is Content Security Policy?
answer: Content Security Policy, or CSP, is a browser security mechanism that allows a site to restrict which sources of scripts, styles, images, connections, and other resources may be loaded or executed. A properly configured CSP can significantly reduce the impact of certain XSS attacks.

title: What is a JavaScript memory leak?
answer: A memory leak occurs when objects that are no longer logically needed remain reachable and therefore cannot be garbage-collected. Common causes include forgotten event listeners, timers, retained DOM references, global collections, and closures that unintentionally retain large objects.

title: How does garbage collection work in JavaScript?
answer: JavaScript engines automatically reclaim memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from relevant live roots. Modern engines use sophisticated garbage-collection strategies, commonly including tracing approaches such as mark-and-sweep and generational techniques.

title: What is reachability in JavaScript garbage collection?
answer: An object is generally considered reachable when it can be accessed through a chain of references from garbage-collection roots, such as active execution contexts or certain global references. Objects that are no longer reachable can eventually be reclaimed by the garbage collector.

title: Can you force garbage collection in normal browser JavaScript?
answer: Normal web-page JavaScript does not provide a standard API for directly forcing garbage collection. JavaScript engines decide when garbage collection should run. Some development environments may provide engine-specific diagnostic options, but application code should not depend on them.

title: What is WeakRef in JavaScript?
answer: WeakRef allows code to hold a weak reference to an object without keeping that object alive solely because of the reference. The object may be garbage-collected at any time, so WeakRef should be used only for specialized caching or memory-sensitive scenarios where nondeterministic availability is acceptable.

title: What is FinalizationRegistry?
answer: FinalizationRegistry allows code to register cleanup-related callbacks associated with objects that become eligible for garbage collection. The timing of such callbacks is nondeterministic, so it should not be used for essential resource management or correctness-critical cleanup.

title: What is a race condition in JavaScript?
answer: A race condition occurs when the result of a program depends on the timing or ordering of asynchronous operations. For example, two API requests may complete in a different order than they were started, causing stale data to overwrite newer data.

title: How can you prevent race conditions in asynchronous JavaScript?
answer: Use appropriate sequencing, cancellation, request identifiers, AbortController, state validation, or concurrency primitives depending on the problem. For search suggestions, for example, a previous request can be aborted or its response can be ignored if it no longer corresponds to the latest query.

title: What is concurrency in JavaScript?
answer: Concurrency means multiple operations can make progress during overlapping periods. JavaScript can coordinate many asynchronous operations through the event loop even though ordinary JavaScript execution on the main thread is single-threaded. Workers can provide additional execution threads for suitable workloads.

title: What is parallelism in JavaScript?
answer: Parallelism means multiple computations execute simultaneously on separate execution resources. In browser JavaScript, Web Workers can enable CPU-intensive computations to run on separate threads, allowing actual parallel execution while communicating with the main thread through messages.

title: What is Promise chaining?
answer: Promise chaining connects asynchronous operations by returning a Promise from a then() callback. The next then() receives the resolved value of that returned Promise. Errors can propagate through the chain to a later catch().

title: What happens when a then() callback returns a normal value?
answer: The next Promise in the chain is fulfilled with that returned value. For example, if a then() callback returns 42, the following then() receives 42.

title: What happens when a then() callback returns a Promise?
answer: The next Promise in the chain adopts the state of the returned Promise. If it fulfills, the next handler receives its value. If it rejects, the rejection propagates through the chain until it is handled.

title: What happens if a Promise executor throws an error?
answer: If the executor function passed to new Promise() throws synchronously, the Promise is automatically rejected with that error. The rejection can then be handled using catch() or an equivalent error-handling mechanism.

title: What is Promise.resolve()?
answer: Promise.resolve() creates a fulfilled Promise for a value or adopts the state of a thenable or Promise passed to it. It is useful for normalizing synchronous values and Promise-like values into a Promise-based interface.

title: What is Promise.reject()?
answer: Promise.reject() creates a Promise that is immediately rejected with the supplied reason. It is useful when implementing Promise-based APIs that need to represent an already-known failure.

title: What is Promise.withResolvers()?
answer: Promise.withResolvers() provides a Promise together with its associated resolve and reject functions without requiring the traditional executor pattern. It can simplify certain APIs that need to expose a Promise while resolving it from external event handlers. It should still be used carefully to avoid unnecessarily exposing control over Promise settlement.

title: What is an unhandled Promise rejection?
answer: An unhandled Promise rejection occurs when a Promise rejects and no appropriate rejection handler is attached. Browsers and JavaScript runtimes can report these through mechanisms such as unhandledrejection or runtime-specific diagnostics. Applications should handle expected failures explicitly.

title: What is the unhandledrejection event?
answer: The unhandledrejection event allows browser code to observe Promise rejections that have not been handled. It can be useful for centralized error reporting, but it should not replace proper local error handling for expected failures.

title: What is queueMicrotask()?
answer: queueMicrotask() schedules a callback to run as a microtask after the current JavaScript execution completes and before the event loop proceeds to the next task. It is useful when work needs microtask timing without creating a Promise solely for scheduling.

title: What is the difference between queueMicrotask() and setTimeout()?
answer: queueMicrotask() schedules work in the microtask queue, which is processed after the current task completes and before the next task. setTimeout() schedules a future task. Therefore, a queued microtask generally runs before a zero-delay timeout scheduled from the same task.

title: What is the difference between microtask starvation and event-loop starvation?
answer: Microtask starvation can occur when code continually schedules more microtasks, preventing the event loop from moving on to other tasks and rendering opportunities. More generally, event-loop starvation occurs when long-running or continuously scheduled work prevents other queued work from receiving execution time. Both can make an application appear unresponsive.

title: What is the difference between Object.is() and ===?
answer: Object.is() is similar to strict equality but handles a few edge cases differently. It considers NaN equal to itself and distinguishes +0 from -0. In contrast, === considers NaN unequal to itself and treats +0 and -0 as equal.

title: What is SameValueZero equality?
answer: SameValueZero is an equality algorithm used by several JavaScript APIs. It considers NaN equal to itself and treats +0 and -0 as equal. Methods such as Array.prototype.includes() and collections such as Set use this comparison behavior in relevant operations.

title: What is the difference between includes() and indexOf()?
answer: includes() returns a boolean and uses SameValueZero comparison, so it can find NaN. indexOf() returns the matching index or -1 and uses strict equality semantics, so indexOf(NaN) does not find NaN.

title: What is the difference between delete and setting a property to undefined?
answer: delete obj.key removes the property from the object. Setting obj.key = undefined keeps the property but changes its value to undefined. This distinction can affect property existence checks, enumeration, and object behavior.

title: What does the delete operator do with array elements?
answer: Using delete on an array element removes the property at that index but does not shift the remaining elements. This creates a sparse array. If you want to remove an element and shift later elements, splice() is generally more appropriate.

title: What is a sparse array?
answer: A sparse array is an array that has missing indexes rather than a value at every position. For example, deleting an array element can create a hole. Some array methods treat holes differently from explicit undefined values.

title: What is the difference between an empty slot and undefined in an array?
answer: An empty slot means the array does not have a property at that index, while an element explicitly containing undefined does have a property whose value is undefined. This difference can be observed using operations such as in, Object.hasOwn(), and certain iteration methods.

title: What is Array.prototype.sort() and what is an important behavior to remember?
answer: sort() sorts the elements of an array in place and returns the same array. By default, values are converted to strings and sorted lexicographically. For numeric sorting, provide a comparator such as (a, b) => a - b.

title: How do you sort numbers correctly in JavaScript?
answer: Provide a numeric comparator to sort(). For ascending order use numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b), and for descending order use numbers.sort((a, b) => b - a). Without a comparator, numbers are sorted as strings.

title: Does sort() mutate the original array?
answer: Yes. sort() modifies the original array in place. If the original array must remain unchanged, create a copy first, such as const sorted = [...items].sort(compareFn).

title: What is toSorted()?
answer: toSorted() provides a non-mutating alternative to sort(). It returns a new sorted array while leaving the original array unchanged. It is useful when working with immutable data patterns.

title: What are toReversed(), toSpliced(), and with()?
answer: These are non-mutating array methods. toReversed() returns a reversed copy, toSpliced() returns a modified copy without changing the original, and with() returns a copy with one element replaced at a specified index. They are useful when immutable updates are preferred.

title: What is the difference between push() and concat()?
answer: push() adds elements to the end of an array and mutates the original array, returning the new length. concat() creates and returns a new array without modifying the original array.

title: What is the difference between push() and unshift()?
answer: push() adds elements to the end of an array, while unshift() adds elements to the beginning. Both mutate the original array. Adding elements at the beginning can require more element movement for large arrays.

title: What is the difference between pop() and shift()?
answer: pop() removes and returns the last element of an array. shift() removes and returns the first element. Both mutate the original array, but removing from the beginning may require shifting the remaining elements.

title: How can you remove duplicate values from an array?
answer: A common approach is [...new Set(array)]. Set stores unique values, and the spread operator converts the Set back into an array. The result preserves the insertion order of the unique values.

title: How do you find duplicate values in an array?
answer: You can use a Set or Map to track values that have already been encountered. For example, while iterating, if a value already exists in a tracking Set, it can be added to a duplicates collection.

title: How do you find the frequency of elements in an array?
answer: A Map or plain object can be used as a frequency counter. Iterate through the array and increment the count for each value. A Map is particularly useful when keys may be values other than strings.

title: How do you group an array of objects by a property?
answer: You can use reduce() to create an object or Map where each property value becomes a group key. Each item is then pushed into the corresponding group. This is a common interview problem involving accumulation and object or Map manipulation.

title: How do you flatten a nested array without using flat()?
answer: You can use recursion with reduce() to recursively process nested arrays. Another approach is to use a stack and repeatedly extract elements until no nested arrays remain. The appropriate implementation depends on the required nesting depth and performance constraints.

title: How do you find the maximum value in an array?
answer: For a numeric array, you can use Math.max(...numbers) for reasonably sized arrays, or use reduce() or a loop for large arrays to avoid spreading a very large number of arguments.

title: How do you find the second-largest number in an array?
answer: An efficient approach is to scan the array once while maintaining the largest and second-largest distinct values. This provides O(n) time complexity and avoids sorting the entire array. The implementation should explicitly define how duplicate maximum values are handled.

title: How do you check whether two arrays are equal?
answer: Comparing arrays with === checks whether they are the same object reference, not whether their contents are equal. For shallow arrays, compare lengths and corresponding elements. For nested structures, a suitable deep-comparison strategy is required.

title: Why does [] === [] return false?
answer: Arrays are objects, and object equality compares references rather than their contents. Two separately created array literals represent two different objects, so [] === [] returns false.

title: Why does {} === {} return false?
answer: Each object literal creates a distinct object reference. Strict equality checks whether both operands refer to the same object, so two separately created object literals are not equal.

title: What is referential equality?
answer: Referential equality means comparing whether two variables refer to the same object or function instance. Operators such as === use reference identity for objects rather than comparing their internal properties.

title: What is structural equality?
answer: Structural equality means determining whether two values have equivalent contents or structure. JavaScript does not provide a universal built-in deep structural equality operator for arbitrary objects, so applications typically use specialized comparison logic or libraries when needed.

title: What is object identity?
answer: Object identity refers to the unique runtime identity of an object. Two objects can contain exactly the same properties and values but still have different identities. Reference equality checks whether two references point to the same object identity.

title: What is a tagged template literal?
answer: A tagged template literal passes a template literal's string segments and interpolated values to a function. The tag function can process, transform, validate, or format the template input before returning a result.

title: What are template literals?
answer: Template literals use backticks and support embedded expressions using ${...}. They also support multiline strings and can be passed to tag functions. They are generally more convenient than traditional string concatenation for dynamic text.

title: What is String.raw()?
answer: String.raw() returns a string using the raw string segments of a template literal, without interpreting escape sequences in those segments in the normal way. It can be useful when working with strings where backslashes need to be preserved.

title: What is Unicode in JavaScript?
answer: JavaScript strings represent text using UTF-16 code units. Many Unicode characters are represented by a single code unit, while characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane may require surrogate pairs. Modern JavaScript provides APIs such as codePointAt() and String.fromCodePoint() for working with Unicode code points.

title: What is the difference between charAt() and bracket notation for strings?
answer: Both can access a character-like position in a string, but bracket notation returns undefined for an out-of-range index, while charAt() returns an empty string. Neither should be assumed to correctly handle every Unicode grapheme as a single character.

title: What is String.prototype.at()?
answer: at() returns the character or element at a specified index and supports negative indexes. For example, str.at(-1) returns the final code unit of the string. It is also available on arrays and other indexed collections that implement the method.

title: What is Intl in JavaScript?
answer: Intl is the internationalization API namespace. It provides functionality for locale-sensitive formatting and comparison, including number formatting, date and time formatting, relative time, plural rules, and collation.

title: What is Intl.NumberFormat?
answer: Intl.NumberFormat formats numbers according to locale and formatting options. It can handle decimal values, percentages, currencies, units, and other locale-sensitive number representations.

title: What is Intl.DateTimeFormat?
answer: Intl.DateTimeFormat formats dates and times according to locale and specified options. It is preferable to manually constructing localized date strings because it handles locale-specific conventions more reliably.

title: What is Intl.Collator?
answer: Intl.Collator provides locale-sensitive string comparison. It is useful for sorting or comparing strings according to language-specific collation rules instead of relying only on basic Unicode code-unit ordering.

title: What is Intl.RelativeTimeFormat?
answer: Intl.RelativeTimeFormat formats relative time values according to locale. For example, it can produce localized representations equivalent to phrases such as 'in 2 days' or '3 hours ago'.

title: What is Intl.PluralRules?
answer: Intl.PluralRules determines the locale-specific plural category for a number, such as one, two, few, many, or other. It is useful for implementing grammatically correct localized messages.

title: What is the difference between Date.now() and new Date()?
answer: Date.now() returns the current time as a numeric timestamp representing milliseconds since the Unix epoch. new Date() creates a Date object representing the current time when called without arguments.

title: What is the Unix timestamp?
answer: A Unix timestamp represents a point in time as an offset from the Unix epoch, which begins at 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. JavaScript Date timestamps are expressed in milliseconds, whereas many systems represent Unix timestamps in seconds.

title: Why can JavaScript Date handling be tricky?
answer: Date handling involves time zones, locale formatting, daylight-saving transitions, parsing rules, and differences between local time and UTC. For reliable applications, dates should be represented and formatted intentionally rather than relying on ambiguous date strings.

title: What is UTC in JavaScript date handling?
answer: UTC is a global time standard independent of local time zones. JavaScript Date objects internally represent an instant as a timestamp, and methods such as getUTCFullYear() and toISOString() allow UTC-based access or formatting.

title: What is the difference between getHours() and getUTCHours()?
answer: getHours() returns the hour according to the local time zone of the environment. getUTCHours() returns the hour according to UTC. The values can differ depending on the local time zone and daylight-saving rules.

title: What is toISOString()?
answer: toISOString() converts a valid Date object into an ISO 8601-style string in UTC, typically such as 2026-08-18T16:30:00.000Z. It is commonly used for interoperable date-time representations in APIs.

title: What is RegExp in JavaScript?
answer: RegExp represents a regular expression used for pattern matching and text processing. Regular expressions can be created using literal syntax such as /pattern/ or with the RegExp constructor.

title: What are common JavaScript regular expression flags?
answer: Common flags include g for global matching, i for case-insensitive matching, m for multiline behavior, s for allowing dot to match line terminators, u for Unicode-aware behavior, y for sticky matching, and d for match indices.

title: What is the difference between match(), matchAll(), search(), and exec()?
answer: match() returns matches according to the regular expression and flags. matchAll() returns an iterator containing detailed match information for global matching. search() returns the index of the first match or -1. exec() executes a regular expression and returns detailed match information or null.

title: What is the difference between greedy and lazy quantifiers in regular expressions?
answer: Greedy quantifiers attempt to match as much text as possible while still allowing the overall pattern to succeed. Lazy quantifiers attempt to match as little as possible. For example, .* is greedy while .*? is lazy.
